units.title: Making the work transferable: a framework, a summary and your own worst objection

lessons.title: A screening framework a colleague can apply without you
lessons.explanation: A framework is not a longer checklist. It is a set of decision rules written so that a different person, working from the same file, reaches the same conclusion and can say why. Four properties make that happen. First, every field names an input, a source and a date: not "deposits" but "total business deposits per the twelve most recent processor statements, dated, named file". A field without a source is an opinion wearing a number's clothes. Second, every field resolves to one of three states rather than two: pass, fail, or unresolved. Unresolved is not a soft pass. It is the default when the evidence is absent, and it blocks exactly as a fail blocks, because the thing that decides a file is the evidence in it, not the merchant's account of the evidence. Third, the framework separates objective fields from judgment fields and locates the judgment in a named person with a written rationale. "Management quality" scored silently by whoever is holding the phone is not a field; the same question scored 1 to 3 by a named reviewer who writes one sentence of support is. Fourth, the framework is dated and versioned, so that a decision made in March can be re-read in October and compared against the rule that was actually in force. The regulatory language for this is borrowed, not owned: the OCC expects a credit risk rating system's assignment criteria to be "clear and precisely defined" using both objective factors (cash flow coverage, debt-to-worth) and subjective ones (quality of management, willingness to repay), expects the ratings to be documented in the credit file, and expects the process to be independently validated and back-tested against outcomes. A broker's screen is not a bank rating system, and no part of that handbook binds a non-bank advisor. What transfers is the design logic: explicit criteria, documented support, independent second look, and a test against what actually happened. A framework is also not a verdict. Its output is a note that says what the file supports, what is missing, and what would change the answer. It never promises that a funder will agree, and the honest version says so in its own text.
lessons.example: Marisol writes a twelve-field screen and tests it before using it on live files. Five fields are objective (months of operating history evidenced by statements in hand; total deposits per those statements; every open obligation with its payoff letter; the disqualifier list checked line by line; whether a UCC search has been run). Three are judgment fields scored 1 to 3 by the reviewer. Four are document fields. She and a colleague screen the same twenty archived files independently, then compare. They agree on 17 of 20, which is 85.00 percent. All three disagreements are in judgment fields; none is in an objective field, which tells her the arithmetic part of the framework travels and the interpretation part does not. The cost of the exercise is straightforward: twenty screens at 1.5 hours each at a $45 hourly opportunity cost is 20 x 1.5 x $45 = $1,350.00, and the three disagreements cost 3 x 0.5 x $45 = $67.50 of rework, which is 5.00 percent of the total. She adds one rule: any judgment field scored at either extreme is read by a second person, a quarter hour each. That is 20 x 0.25 x $45 = $225.00, lifting the cost to $1,575.00, an increase of 16.67 percent over $1,350.00, and lifting agreement to 19 of 20, or 95.00 percent. She writes both figures into the framework's version note, because a colleague deserves to know what the rule costs before being asked to follow it. The framework's first live use produces a two-line output on a file she would once have submitted: three fields unresolved, so the note says the amount the supplied evidence supports and names the three documents that would move those fields to pass or fail.
lessons.question: A colleague runs the screen on a merchant who says he has been operating for two years but supplies statements for three months. Under a framework with a pass / fail / unresolved rule, what is the correct output and why?
lessons.answer: Unresolved on the tenure field, which blocks the same way a fail blocks; the note records the merchant's statement as a claim, names the statement months that would resolve the field, and states the amount the evidence in hand supports.
lessons.distractor: Pass on tenant tenure because the merchant has been in business two years and the statements are only a formality, so the screen can continue to the amount question.
lessons.correction: A framework with a two-state rule collapses "I have not seen it" into "it is fine", which is the failure the unresolved state exists to prevent. The merchant's statement is a claim about the file; the statements are the file. Recording the claim while marking the field unresolved keeps both facts visible and leaves the decision where it belongs, on evidence, while the note still gives the merchant something to do. Note that this is not the same as rejecting the file: unresolved fields have a clearance path, and the note should carry it.

depth.definitions: A screen is a non-binding, evidence-based pre-assessment performed before an application; it creates no obligation and should involve no inquiry that affects credit standing. A field is one question with a defined input and source. A threshold is the value at which a field changes state, written down in advance. Pass, fail and unresolved are the three states; unresolved is the default wherever the source is missing, undated or inconsistent. A blocking field is one whose fail or unresolved state ends the screen as a decline or a not-yet. Inter-rater agreement is the share of files on which two reviewers reach the same state, field by field or file by file, and it is the practical test of whether a framework travels. Versioning is the practice of dating the rule set so an old decision can be audited against the rule then in force. Back-testing compares the framework's past states against what actually happened to those files.
depth.mechanism: Written criteria transfer because they move reasoning out of a person and into a document that can be inspected, argued with and improved. Tacit judgment fails in two directions at once: it cannot be checked, so a wrong call looks the same as a right one, and it cannot be tuned, because nobody can see which step produced the error. A three-state rule addresses the specific information problem of pre-application screening. The party with the weaker information, the merchant, bears the cost of a failed attempt, while the party with the stronger information, the advisor, is paid only on a funded transaction. A two-state rule systematically converts missing evidence into a submit decision and pushes the cost downstream. The independent-validation idea borrowed from supervisory practice supplies the second mechanism: a rule that nobody else applies is a preference, and the only way to find out which it is, is to hand the same files to someone else and compare. Disagreement inside an objective field means the framework is ambiguous and should be rewritten; disagreement inside a judgment field means the scoring scale or the reviewer's support sentence is inadequate. Those two diagnoses have opposite fixes, which is why the objective and judgment fields must be kept apart in the document itself.
depth.secondExample: The contrasting failure is a framework that is too granular, and it fails in the opposite direction from a framework that is too thin. A second advisor writes a twenty-two field screen, of which fourteen require documents that a merchant in the first thirty days of a relationship typically does not have. On the same twenty archived files, fourteen of twenty-two fields come back unresolved, a rate of 63.64 percent, and the median screen takes 3.5 hours rather than 1.5, which is 3.5 x $45 = $157.50 per file against $67.50, an increase of 133.33 percent. Agreement is high, 19 of 20, but the framework has stopped screening and started documenting: almost every file lands in not-yet, the advisor's time is spent requesting paper, and the merchant experiences the framework as a queue. The repair is not to delete fields but to sort them: the three fields that actually change decisions stay in the screen, the document fields become a named clearance list attached to the note, and the remaining fields are moved to a post-application checklist where the funder's own process will ask for them anyway. Two files that were previously not-yet resolve to a defensible yes with a clearance condition, which is the outcome the screen was built to produce.
depth.mistake: The common mistake is treating disagreement as a discipline problem and tightening the thresholds until everyone agrees, which buys agreement by destroying the field's information. The diagnostic is which kind of field produced the disagreement. If two reviewers read the same dated statement and reach different states, the framework's wording is ambiguous and the field should be split into observable parts, for example replacing "management quality" with "years of owner experience in this industry", "demonstrated response to a prior shortfall", and "whether the owner answered the document request in the stated time". If they read the same statement and reach the same state but write different rationale sentences, the fix is a support-sentence template, not a threshold change. A related mistake is using the framework's own output as evidence of quality, for example citing a 95 percent agreement figure to a merchant or a funder as if it were a credit judgment. Agreement measures whether the rule travels between people; it says nothing about whether the rule is any good, which only back-testing against outcomes can say.
depth.application: Task: write a twelve-field screen for the files you actually see, split into objective, judgment and document fields, with a source and a date rule for each; then have a colleague run it independently on three archived files you have already decided. Deliverables: the one-page framework with a version date; the two independent result sheets; a list of every disagreement labelled as objective or judgment; and a one-paragraph change note with the cost of the change computed in hours and dollars. Self-review rubric: does every field name an input and a source (not a feeling); does every field have a written in-advance threshold; is unresolved the stated default where evidence is missing; is each judgment field scored by a named person with one support sentence; does the framework state in its own text that it is a screen rather than a decision and that it never predicts a funder's answer; and can a colleague who has never seen your files reproduce your states from the documents alone? If the third file produces a different state on an objective field, fix the wording before using the framework live.
depth.summary: A framework is the smallest durable unit of advising: the reasoning written down so it can be handed over, checked, and improved rather than re-derived from scratch each time. The three-state rule, the source-and-date requirement, the objective and judgment split, versioning and a second reader together convert individual judgement into a process whose failures are visible. Held correctly, the framework also states its own limits: it supports a note about what a file can carry, never a promise that a funder will agree, and its value is measured by whether it predicted outcomes, not by how confidently it was applied.

readings.title: eCFR - 13 CFR 120.150, What are SBA's lending criteria?
readings.note: Read all of it; it is four sentences. The applicant must be creditworthy, loans must be so sound as to reasonably assure repayment, and lenders and CDCs must use appropriate and prudent generally acceptable commercial credit analysis processes and procedures consistent with those used for their similarly-sized non-SBA guaranteed loans; criteria that may be considered are credit score or credit history of the applicant, its Associates and any guarantors, earnings or cashflow, and where applicable equity or collateral (as amended, 88 FR 21085, 10 April 2023). Section-specific direction: this is the authoritative statement that fundability rests on repayment capacity and history, which is what a screen's objective fields must model. visual.title: Three-state screening: how one field routes a file and how the framework is tested
visual.description: A labeled sequence showing a twelve-field screen in which every field resolves to pass, fail or unresolved, with unresolved blocking like a fail, and showing the two-reviewer test that decides whether the framework can be handed over.
steps: Field block one - objective: operating history in months, total deposits per dated statements, every open obligation with a payoff figure, the disqualifier list, and whether a UCC search has been run. Each line shows the source document and its date.
Field block two - judgment: three fields scored 1 to 3 by a named reviewer, each with one support sentence written at the time of scoring.
Gates: pass continues; fail ends the screen as a decline with a reason; unresolved ends it as not-yet and adds the field to a named clearance list with the document that would resolve it.
Version line: framework title, version number and date, so a decision made in March can be re-read against the rule in force in March.

Test line: two reviewers run the same twenty archived files; agreement is recorded by field type, and every disagreement is labelled objective (rewrite the wording) or judgment (template or training), with the cost of any added step computed in hours and dollars.

lessons.title: Writing a file summary a credit committee can act on
lessons.explanation: A file summary exists so that someone who has never spoken to the merchant can decide, or decide against, in a single sitting. That sets the shape. The decision requested goes at the top, in one sentence, with the amount, the instrument, the term and the conditions: "approve $35,000 at $134 per $100 of net proceeds over 26 weeks, conditional on a UCC search and three additional statement months." Everything below exists to support or defeat that sentence. The OCC's write-up standard is a good template even for a non-bank file, because it was designed for a reader who is not permitted to take the writer's word: a heading that identifies the borrower, the amounts and any guarantors; a credit description with facility type, origination, repayment terms, maturity, purpose, collateral and source of repayment; a financial information section that presents conclusions rather than transcribing statements; an analysis section that states the cause of any weakness and the effect on repayment capacity, the current repayment source or the absence of one, the external factors that bear on the decision, and what management has or has not done; and a conclusion that gives the reasons and any instructions. Two rules from that standard matter more than the sections themselves. The first is that the essential test of the summary is whether it supports the decision: a paragraph that does not change the answer and does not evidence the answer belongs in the file, not in the memo. The second is that details recited at length weaken rather than strengthen: a memo listing fourteen ratios has not done the work of deciding which two of them carry the file. A committee-acting summary therefore states the two or three facts that carry the decision, the arithmetic behind the amount, the conditions, and the assumption that would reverse the recommendation, and it separates what is known from what is assumed. It also names the writer's own position in the transaction where the reader would otherwise have to guess. A summary that ends with "looks good" gives a committee nothing to approve and nothing to refuse.
lessons.example: Riverton Truck Repair asks for $85,000. The file shows $74,000 in monthly deposits across the twelve most recent statements, an existing equipment loan at $2,400 a week, 3.2 years of trading, a clean UCC search, and no disqualifying activity. Weekly deposits are $74,000 x 12 / 52 = $17,076.92. At a 38 percent contribution margin, weekly contribution is 17,076.92 x 0.38 = $6,489.23, and the existing obligation is 2,400 / 6,489.23 = 36.98 percent of contribution before anything new is added. The requested $85,000 at a factor of 1.34 is $113,900 over 26 weeks, or 113,900 / 26 = $4,380.77 a week. Combined with the existing loan that is 4,380.77 + 2,400 = $6,780.77 against $6,489.23 of contribution: a coverage ratio of 6,489.23 / 6,780.77 = 0.96, which is below one, meaning the merchant's contribution does not cover the combined remittances in an average week. Under the house rule that combined remittances stay at or under 65 percent of contribution, the allowed combined figure is 6,489.23 x 0.65 = $4,218.00, leaving room of 4,218.00 - 2,400 = $1,818.00 a week. At a factor of 1.34 over 26 weeks that supports 1,818.00 x 26 / 1.34 = $35,274.63 of net proceeds, so the memo recommends $35,000: 35,000 x 1.34 = $46,900, or $1,803.85 a week, which is $134 per $100 of net proceeds, with combined remittances of $4,203.85 at 64.78 percent of contribution and a coverage ratio of 1.54. The memo states the request, the recommendation, the two facts that carry it (deposits per dated statements, the existing obligation per a payoff figure), the arithmetic above, three conditions (a UCC search, the payoff letter, and the six months of statements still missing), the reversal assumption (a fall in deposits of more than one third, which is where coverage reaches one), and the writer's compensation on the transaction. It also names what is not in the file: no interim financial statements and no personal financial statement. The memo takes 90 minutes at a $45 opportunity cost, $67.50, against the merchant's equipment discount of 2.5 percent on a $74,000 unit, $1,850, which is what a week of avoidable committee round-trips would put at risk.
lessons.question: A draft memo lists fourteen ratios, five pages of statement excerpts and a conclusion that says the file "looks good" without naming a figure. What is the single most important repair?
lessons.answer: Put the decision requested at the top with amount, term, per-hundred-dollars cost, conditions and the one assumption that would reverse it, then cut everything that neither supports nor defeats that sentence.
lessons.distractor: Add a fifteenth ratio and an appendix of the full statements so the committee has the complete record and can reach its own conclusion from the raw data.
lessons.correction: Completeness is not the test; support is. The OCC's write-up standard says the essential test of a write-up is whether it supports the rating, and that reciting details from statements rather than presenting conclusions from them detracts. A committee cannot act on a memo that has not decided anything, and adding data lengthens the meeting rather than shortening it. The repair is subtraction plus a decision line: which two or three facts carry the file, what arithmetic turns them into an amount, what is assumed, and what would make the writer reverse.

depth.definitions: A file summary, a credit write-up and a committee memo are the same artefact under different names: a document that lets a decision-maker act without direct contact with the merchant. Coverage ratio, in this course, is weekly contribution divided by weekly combined remittances; a value below one means the average week's contribution does not cover the combined obligation. Contribution margin is the share of receipts left after direct costs, stated as a percentage, and it is an estimate that must be labelled as one. Per-hundred-dollars cost is total repayment divided by net proceeds, multiplied by one hundred, which is a commercial financing convention and not an annual percentage rate. Net proceeds are the amount the merchant actually receives after fees deducted or withheld at disbursement; the gross advance is the larger number before those deductions. Conditions are the evidence or events that must exist before funding; the reversal assumption is the single measured change that turns a yes into a no.
depth.mechanism: A committee is an attention budget, not a source of extra analysis. Its decisions get better when the memo front-loads the decision and the two facts that carry it, because a reviewer who must reconstruct the writer's reasoning will either rubber-stamp or reach for the largest number on the page, and neither is a credit decision. The write-up standard's insistence on stating the cause of a problem rather than merely describing the problem is the operational core of this: "deposits fell 14 percent" is an observation, while "deposits fell because the largest customer moved to a competitor in June, and nothing in the file replaces that volume" is an analysis a reviewer can test against evidence. Separating known from assumed does the same work at a different level, because it tells the reviewer exactly where a challenge will land. A memo that hides its assumptions is not more persuasive; it is merely harder to attack until the moment someone asks a question in the meeting, at which point the cost of the omission is the meeting itself.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting file shows the same structure producing a not-yet rather than a yes, which is where summaries earn their keep. Hollis Sign & Awning asks for $120,000. Weekly deposits compute to $58,400 x 12 / 52 = $13,476.92, contribution at 31 percent is $4,177.85, and existing debits are $2,050 a week, which is 49.07 percent of contribution before anything new. The requested structure is $120,000 at a factor of 1.35 over 26 weeks = $162,000 / 26 = $6,230.77 a week, which combined with the existing debits is $8,280.77 against $4,177.85 of contribution, a coverage ratio of 0.50. There is no pricing conversation that closes a gap of that shape; a lower factor would still leave coverage below one, and the honest memo says so in one line rather than opening a negotiation. What the file does support is a working-capital advance of roughly $25,000 over 26 weeks at a factor of 1.35, which is 25,000 x 1.35 / 26 = $1,298.08 a week, combined $3,348.08, 80.14 percent of contribution and coverage of 1.25. The memo therefore contains two decisions: a decline of the request as structured, with the coverage arithmetic as the reason, and a conditional recommendation of the smaller figure, with the conditions and the reversal assumption attached. The merchant is entitled to both lines in writing, because a committee memo that only says no leaves the merchant with nothing to act on.
depth.mistake: The most common error is writing the memo for the merchant rather than for the reviewer: omitting the writer's compensation, softening the weaknesses, and describing conditions as paperwork rather than as decision points. The diagnostic is to read the memo asking two questions, what does the writer get paid if this funds, and what single measured change would make this writer refuse. If either answer is absent, the memo is advocacy rather than a decision document. A second error is burying the reversal assumption in the analysis section; it belongs in the conclusion, in its own line, because it is the sentence a hostile reviewer will quote. A third is presenting an estimated contribution margin as if it were a measured figure: state the percentage, say it is an estimate, and name the basis, for example two years of statements plus the merchant's own cost schedule.
depth.application: Task: write a one-page summary for a file you have screened, with the decision line first, a credit description of six lines or fewer, a financial section that presents conclusions rather than reciting statements, an analysis that names the cause of any weakness and its effect on repayment, a conclusion with reasons, conditions, the per-hundred-dollars cost and the reversal assumption, and a line stating the writer's own compensation and its contingency. Then give it to a colleague who has not seen the file and ask them to state the decision and the one thing that would change it. Self-review rubric: can the reviewer state the decision without asking a question; is every figure traceable to a named document and date; are known and assumed separated; is net proceeds distinguished from the gross advance; is no factor presented as a rate or an APR; does the memo contain at least one condition that could not be waved through; and does it say plainly that nothing in it constitutes an approval.
depth.summary: A summary converts scattered evidence into a decision that a stranger can make and defend in a single sitting. Its discipline is subtractive: state the decision, the two or three facts that carry it, the arithmetic that turns those facts into an amount, the conditions, the reversal assumption, and the writer's interest. Written that way it does more than inform a committee; it creates a record that a reviewer, a regulator, or the merchant can test later, and it makes the writer's own conflict visible instead of discovering it in a meeting.

readings.title: OCC Comptroller's Handbook - Rating Credit Risk: Appendix B (Write-Up Standards, Guidelines, and Examples)
readings.note: Read the whole of Appendix B. It lists the five write-up components - heading, credit description, financial information, analysis, conclusion - and the content expected under each, including repayment terms, maturity, purpose, collateral with the most recent valuation and its date, source of repayment, delinquency and accrual status, the cause of any credit problem, the current repayment source or the absence of one, actions management took or failed to take, and the reasons for the rating. Read the instruction to present conclusions derived from the financial information rather than recite details from statements, and the sentence that "the essential test of a good write-up is whether it supports the rating". Section-specific direction: use Appendix B as the structural template for a committee-facing file summary, including its allowance for a narrative or bullet format. readings.title: FDIC Risk Management Manual of Examination Policies, Section 3.2 - Loans (Loan Review Systems; Credit Risk Rating or Grading Systems)
readings.note: Read "Loan Review Systems" and the first paragraphs of "Credit Risk Rating or Grading Systems". Read also the sentence that a loan officer's judgment about a credit grade should generally be subject to review, which is why a summary must be written to be challenged. visual.title: The committee-facing summary: decision first, support second, assumption last
visual.description: A labeled layout of a one-page file summary showing the order that lets a reviewer decide in one sitting, with the arithmetic that converts deposits into a supportable amount and the line that names what would reverse it.
steps: Line one - decision requested: amount, instrument, term, per-hundred-dollars cost of net proceeds, conditions and the date the decision is needed by.
Block two - the two or three facts that carry it: each with a named document and date, for example deposits per the twelve most recent statements and the existing obligation per its payoff letter.

Block three - the arithmetic: monthly deposits x 12 / 52 to weekly; weekly x contribution margin to contribution; existing weekly debits; allowed combined remittances at the stated floor; the amount that floor supports at the quoted factor.
Block four - analysis: the cause of any weakness and its effect on repayment capacity, the current repayment source or its absence, and external factors that bear on the decision.
Block five - conclusion: reasons, conditions that must be met before funding, the single measured reversal assumption, and the writer's own compensation and what it depends on.
Footer line - what the file does not contain, and a statement that nothing here is an approval, a rate, or a promise of funds.

lessons.title: A product problem or a pricing problem: diagnosing before you restructure
lessons.explanation: Almost every merchant who is unhappy about cost opens with price, and almost every deal that fails was never a price problem. The distinction is diagnostic and it decides what you are allowed to do next. A product problem is a mismatch between the money and the use: the repayment period does not match how the money pays itself back, the repayment source is not identified, the schedule starts before the money is put to work, or the amount exceeds what the use can carry. A pricing problem is when the structure already fits and the only open question is what the money costs. The supervisory vocabulary for the first category is structural weakness, and the OCC's list is unusually practical: an indefinite or speculative purpose; an indefinite or overly liberal repayment program, including bullet maturities unrelated to the actual source of repayment funds and repayment plans significantly in excess of the useful life of the asset being financed; inadequate debt service coverage; and nonexistent, weak or waived covenants. The same handbook adds the sentence that matters most for a broker's conduct: when competition or other pressures cause a lender to weaken its underwriting and structural protections, credit risk increases, and fundamental underwriting flaws should not go uncriticised because they have become the competitive norm. The diagnostic order is therefore fixed. First, is the purpose definite and does the money get used when the schedule says it will? Second, what repays this, in what amounts, in what weeks? Third, does the coverage floor hold in a normal month and in a bad one? Only fourth do you discuss cost. Restructuring comes in three forms and they are not interchangeable: a different instrument (an amortising term facility for a long-lived asset), a different amount (smaller, so the schedule fits the use), or a different schedule shape (a share-of-receipts structure or a longer period, where the rules allow). Cutting the factor is not restructuring. A discount on a structurally wrong deal buys a few percentage points of repayment and leaves the mismatch intact, which converts an underwriting problem into a predictable loss with a nicer-looking quote attached to it. Duration is a real constraint rather than a preference: the SBA's own programme table puts 7(a) maturities at 10 years or less unless the loan finances or refinances real estate or equipment with a useful life exceeding 10 years, and 504 at 25 years for real estate and 10 for equipment. Whatever the product, the question is the same: does the repayment period sit inside the life of what it bought?
lessons.example: Larkspur Bakery needs $40,000 to replace a deck oven with a twelve-year useful life, and asks for a 20-week advance because that is what it has been offered. Weekly contribution is $3,450 after direct costs. The advance at a factor of 1.32 is $40,000 x 1.32 = $52,800 over 20 weeks, or $2,640 a week, which is $132 per $100 of net proceeds and 2,640 / 3,450 = 76.52 percent of contribution, with a coverage ratio of 3,450 / 2,640 = 1.31. That last figure is why the first conversation goes wrong: 1.31 looks acceptable, so the file is treated as priced rather than badly structured. Now test the price hypothesis directly. The offer improves to a factor of 1.26, a 4.55 percent reduction in amount repaid: $40,000 x 1.26 = $50,400 over 20 weeks is $2,520 a week, $126 per $100, 73.04 percent of contribution, coverage 1.37. Six percentage points of repayment bought four points of coverage, and the structure is untouched: a twelve-year asset is still being repaid out of twenty weeks of receipts, which means the merchant is repaying from working capital rather than from the asset's productive life. The instrument test produces a different answer. On an illustrative term facility at a 9.00 percent note rate over 120 months, $40,000 amortises at $506.70 a month, $60,804.00 in total payments and $20,804.00 of interest, which is $152.01 per $100 of net proceeds: more expensive in total dollars and entirely sustainable in cash terms, because each month's payment is 3.39 percent of a month's contribution (506.70 against $14,950.00 if receipts are steady). The amount test produces a third answer: if the bakery's real need this quarter is working capital rather than a machine, then $18,000 at a factor of 1.30 over 26 weeks is $23,400 / 26 = $900 a week, $130 per $100, which is 26.09 percent of contribution and coverage of 3.83. Three answers, one file, and only the first is a price conversation. The quoted factor is never described as a rate or an annual percentage rate anywhere in the comparison; the term facility's 9.00 percent is an illustrative note rate on a hypothetical loan, not a market quote, and it is labelled that way in the memo.
lessons.question: A merchant's file shows a repayment period of 20 weeks for equipment with a 12-year useful life, a coverage ratio of 1.31 and a requested discount from a factor of 1.32 to 1.26. What should the advisor do?
lessons.answer: Treat it as a product problem: state that the repayment period sits far outside the life of the asset and the use it funds, test an instrument and an amount that match the duration, and leave price as the last item once the structure fits.
lessons.distractor: Negotiate the discount to 1.26 because a coverage ratio above one means the file services comfortably and the merchant's only real objection is the cost.
lessons.correction: Coverage above one rules out a capacity problem in an average week; it says nothing about whether the schedule matches the use. A twelve-year asset repaid over twenty weeks is still being repaid from working capital, and the discount moves the amount repaid by 4.55 percent while leaving that mismatch exactly where it was. Structure first, amount second, price last; and where the instrument changes, say plainly that a term facility at an illustrative note rate is not a rate comparison against a factor, because those are different metrics that cannot be lined up side by side.

depth.definitions: A structural weakness is an underwriting deficiency that compromises the ability to control the credit if events turn adverse, as distinct from a weakness in the borrower's finances. Purpose definiteness means the money has a stated use, an amount and a date. Duration matching means the repayment period sits inside the productive life of what is financed. Coverage ratio here is weekly contribution divided by weekly combined remittances. A bullet maturity is a facility whose principal falls due in one payment unrelated to the timing of the funds that will repay it. Restructuring means changing instrument, amount or schedule shape; repricing means changing only the cost. Per-hundred-dollars cost is total repayment divided by net proceeds times one hundred, a commercial convention and not an annual percentage rate.
depth.mechanism: Pricing and structure fail in different ways, which is why the diagnosis must come first. Price changes the slope of a repayment curve that already fits the cash cycle; structure changes whether the curve can be paid at all. When a schedule is duration-mismatched, the payments come out of working capital, so the merchant's ability to fund inventory, payroll and trade terms degrades in exactly the period the financed asset is supposed to be raising output. That failure is slow and then abrupt, and a discount makes it look better for a few weeks. There is also a behavioural mechanism: a merchant who has been offered a discount experiences the problem as solved, so the real conversation, about instrument or amount, becomes harder to have later. The reverse error exists too, and it is worth naming so the diagnosis is not used as a sales tool: if the structure fits, coverage holds in a bad month, and the source of repayment is identified, then continuing to talk about structure instead of cost is avoidance, and the merchant is entitled to a straight answer about what the money costs in dollars per hundred of net proceeds.
depth.secondExample: The contrasting case is a file where the product is right and the price is genuinely the problem, and treating it as structural would be the error. A commercial cleaning company with four years of receipts asks for $30,000 of working capital to bridge a 90-day receivable cycle from one large client. The use is definite, the repayment source is that receivable, and the timing matches: the money is spent over three months and repaid over them. Weekly receipts average $31,000 and contribution at 34 percent is $10,540; the offer is $30,000 at a factor of 1.35 over 26 weeks, which is $40,500 / 26 = $1,557.69 a week, 14.78 percent of contribution, coverage 6.77. Nothing is structurally wrong: an amortising 26-week schedule sits comfortably inside the 90-day cycle plus a tail. Now the price question is real, because the merchant has a second offer at a factor of 1.29 from a funder with a longer relationship. The comparison is a dollars-per-hundred comparison of the same metric: $135 per $100 of net against $129 per $100 of net, on $30,000 that is $40,500 against $38,700, a difference of $1,800, or $69.23 a week over 26 weeks. The advisor can state that honestly, name their own commission and its contingency, and let the merchant choose. The lesson is symmetrical: refusing to discuss price when the structure is sound is as much a failure of service as restructuring when the problem was cost.
depth.mistake: The most common mistake is treating a high per-hundred-dollars cost as the definition of a bad deal and a low one as the definition of a good deal, which is how a 20-week advance on a 12-year asset gets described as acceptable because the factor is competitive. The diagnostic is to ask what repays this and when, before asking what it costs. A closely related error is comparing a factor with a note rate directly, either by annualising the factor, which produces a number that is not an interest rate, or by presenting a term loan's note rate as if the two were alternatives at the same cost. The correction is to keep the metrics in their own lanes: dollars per hundred of net and total repayment for a purchase of receivables, monthly payment, total payments and interest for an amortising facility, and duration and repayment source for both. A third error is accepting the merchant's stated purpose at face value when the request pattern says something else; a request for equipment money that coincides with a payroll shortfall is a purpose question, not a price question.
depth.application: Task: take one live or archived file and write a one-page structural diagnosis before any pricing discussion. Include the stated purpose with its date, the repayment source and its timing in weeks, the instrument's repayment period against the useful life of what is financed, the coverage ratio in a normal month and in the file's worst recorded month, and three candidate structures (instrument, amount, schedule shape) with the per-hundred-dollars cost of each and no annualised figure anywhere. Then write the two-sentence version you would say to the merchant. Self-review rubric: does the diagnosis name the mismatch in one sentence a merchant would understand; is every structure costed in its own metric rather than converted into a single rate number; is the illustrative note rate labelled illustrative; does the page state that no approval is promised; and does it say what would make you conclude there is no structure that fits, so the honest answer is not-yet?
depth.summary: Diagnosing before restructuring is what keeps a financing conversation honest, because the two problems have different fixes and only one of them is negotiable. Purpose, source, timing and coverage come first; instrument, amount and schedule shape are the tools; price is the last variable, negotiated only once the structure would actually be paid out of the money it funds. Used the other way round, the same vocabulary becomes a way to sell a discount as a solution, which is the failure the OCC names when it warns that a structural weakness does not stop being one because it has become the competitive norm.

readings.note: Read Appendix F in full. It defines structural weaknesses as underwriting deficiencies that can compromise the ability to control a credit relationship if events turn adverse, and lists the prevalent ones: indefinite or speculative purpose; indefinite or overly liberal repayment program, with the indicators being bullet maturities unrelated to the actual source of repayment funds, rewrites or renewals that merely defer a maturity, loans financing asset purchases with a repayment plan significantly in excess of the useful life of the asset, and advances to fund interest payments; nonexistent, weak or waived covenants; and inadequate debt service coverage, which should provide an acceptable margin to repay in a reasonable time. visual.title: Diagnose first: purpose, source, timing, coverage, then price
visual.description: A labeled decision sequence that separates structural mismatches from cost questions, showing how a low-looking coverage ratio can mask a duration mismatch and how a discount changes nothing structural.
steps: Step one - purpose: state the use, its amount and the date the money is actually spent. An indefinite or speculative purpose stops the sequence.
Step two - source: name what repays this, in dollars and in weeks; if the answer is working capital rather than the financed asset's output, the asset question is open.
Step three - duration: compare the repayment period with the useful life of what is financed, using a published reference such as the SBA programme maturity table rather than an assumption.
Step four - coverage: weekly contribution against weekly combined remittances in an average month and in the worst recorded month. Below one in the bad month, the amount is the question.
Step five - structure options: instrument, amount, schedule shape. Cost each in its own metric, dollars per hundred of net proceeds or monthly payment and total payments.
Step six - price last, and only if steps one to five hold. A discount applied to a structural weakness is shown on the diagram as an arrow that changes the slope of the curve and not its shape.

lessons.title: Stress-testing your own recommendation before a reviewer does
lessons.explanation: Every recommendation rests on assumptions, and the ones that sink a file are almost never the ones the advisor wrote down. Stress-testing is the discipline of listing the assumptions, giving each a number and a source, and then changing one at a time to see whether the recommendation survives. Supervisory practice supplies the vocabulary. The Federal Reserve and the OCC describe effective challenge as critical analysis by objective, informed parties who can identify limitations and produce appropriate changes, and they note that effective challenge depends on a combination of incentives, competence and influence: a reviewer with none of the three changes nothing, and an advisor with no habit of challenging themselves supplies none of the three on their own file. That guidance names two ways a model, or a recommendation, goes wrong: it can have fundamental errors and produce inaccurate outputs against its design objective, or it can be used inappropriately or with a misunderstanding of its limitations and assumptions. Applied to a funding recommendation, the second failure is far more common. Nobody's arithmetic is usually wrong; the file is instead run on a deposit figure from a strong quarter, a contribution margin taken from a good month, and a schedule that starts in the busy season. Validation practice suggests three tests. Conceptual soundness: are the inputs the right ones for the decision, and is the contribution margin the merchant's own or a borrowed average? Ongoing monitoring: has anything changed in the file since the numbers were gathered, particularly product mix, one large customer or a new obligation? Outcomes analysis: when you look back at files you decided, do the ones you said would be tight actually have a payment history that shows it? The practical output of all this is one sentence that every recommendation should carry: the assumption that, if wrong in a measured way, would reverse this decision. Say it in numbers, not adjectives. "The recommendation holds unless weekly receipts fall below $20,333.33" is a testable statement; "the merchant's business is stable" is not.
lessons.example: Harborline Print Group: monthly receipts of $112,000 across twelve months, a contribution margin estimated at 30 percent from two years of financial statements plus the owner's cost schedule, existing debits of $2,600 a week, and a request for $70,000. Weekly receipts are 112,000 x 12 / 52 = $25,846.15, contribution is 25,846.15 x 0.30 = $7,753.85, and the offer at a factor of 1.30 over 26 weeks is 70,000 x 1.30 / 26 = $3,500.00 a week, which is $130 per $100 of net proceeds. Combined remittances are 3,500 + 2,600 = $6,100.00, which is 78.67 percent of contribution, and coverage is 7,753.85 / 6,100 = 1.27. Before defending that, the advisor runs four tests and records each one. Test one, one-variable sensitivity: receipts down 15 percent gives weekly receipts of $21,969.23, contribution of $6,590.77, and coverage of 1.08; down 25 percent gives $19,384.62, $5,815.38 and coverage of 0.95, a shortfall of $284.62 a week, which repeats every week of the schedule. Test two, the reversal point computed rather than eyeballed: coverage reaches one when contribution equals $6,100.00, which requires weekly receipts of 6,100 / 0.30 = $20,333.33, or $88,111.11 a month, a decline of 21.33 percent from the figure on which the file was built. Test three, the start date: the schedule begins in the first week of September and the file's own statements show September and October run 24 percent below the annual average, which puts contribution at $5,892.92 and coverage at 0.97 in the first nine weeks, a shortfall of $207.08 a week. Test four, outcomes analysis: the advisor pulls the last fifteen files decided on a similar margin and finds five where the first three months ran below the forecast, three of which needed a schedule adjustment. That is a 33.33 percent hit rate on the tight cases, and it is enough to change the recommendation rather than the arithmetic: the memo now proposes $55,000 over 26 weeks at the same factor, which is 55,000 x 1.30 / 26 = $2,750.00 a week, combined $5,350.00, 68.99 percent of contribution, coverage 1.45 at the baseline and 1.10 in the September-October trough. Nothing about the file changed; the recommendation changed because the assumption was tested before a reviewer tested it.
lessons.question: Your recommendation has a coverage ratio of 1.27 on the annual average and 0.97 in the two months the schedule starts in. What is the correct response?
lessons.answer: Size the amount and match the schedule's start to the cash cycle so the trough is covered, and record the reversal point in the summary as a number rather than defending the average.
lessons.distractor: Keep the amount and rely on the merchant's two strong quarters, since the annual average is the figure the funder's own analysis will use and coverage above one is the standard being applied.
lessons.correction: A schedule is paid week by week, not on an annual average. If the first nine weeks run at the file's recorded seasonal low, the merchant funds the difference from working capital precisely when receipts are lowest, and the average that made the file look comfortable has no bearing on those weeks. The repair is arithmetic, not rhetoric: reduce the amount to what the trough supports, or change the schedule shape, and state the reversal point and the seasonal evidence in the summary so a reviewer can test the same figures.

depth.definitions: An assumption is an input the recommendation depends on that is not itself verified by a source document; a forecast is an assumption about the future. Sensitivity is the change in an output caused by a stated change in one input. The reversal point is the value of an input at which the decision changes, stated in the input's own units. A trough is the lowest recorded period of receipts in the file's history, as distinct from a projection. Effective challenge is critical analysis by objective, informed parties able to identify limitations and produce change, and it depends on incentives, competence and influence. Outcomes analysis compares past decisions with what actually happened; back-testing is outcomes analysis on a sample period not used to build the rule.
depth.mechanism: Stress-testing works because a recommendation is a claim about a range of futures and the summary usually presents only one point inside it. Changing one input at a time isolates the assumption that carries the decision, which is the information a reviewer needs and which a bundle of simultaneous adjustments destroys. The seasonal mechanism is the most common and the most mechanical: a fixed weekly remittance is flat while receipts are not, so the ratio between them varies across the year even when the annual total is exactly as forecast, and a schedule that begins in a peak month will spend its first weeks collecting the merchant's working capital rather than the business's receipts. The outcomes mechanism supplies the base rate that judgement alone cannot: how often files with this shape actually ran tight is a measurable fact about an advisor's own decisions, and it converts a vague worry into a proportion that can be argued with. Recording the reversal point has a second effect that is easy to miss: it makes the recommendation falsifiable in advance, so that a later shortfall is evidence about the file rather than a surprise about the advisor.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting stress test shows the recommendation surviving, and saying so plainly is part of the skill. Corrigan Feeds: monthly receipts of $210,000, contribution at 22 percent because the business is a distributor with thin margins, existing debits of $4,100 a week, seasonal peak in the harvest months and a recorded trough 12 percent below average. Weekly receipts are 210,000 x 12 / 52 = $48,461.54 and contribution is $10,661.54. The offer is $90,000 at a factor of 1.32 over 30 weeks, which is 90,000 x 1.32 / 30 = $3,960.00 a week, $132 per $100 of net, combined with existing debits $8,060.00, which is 75.60 percent of contribution, coverage 1.32. Now stress it properly. A 20 percent fall in receipts, far beyond the recorded 12 percent trough, gives weekly receipts of $38,769.23, contribution of $8,529.23, and coverage of $8,529.23 / $8,060 = 1.06. The reversal point is weekly receipts of 8,060 / 0.22 = $36,636.36, or a 24.40 percent decline from the baseline, which is twice the worst year in the file. On those figures the advisor's honest conclusion is that the recommendation holds and that the reversal assumption, a fall in receipts of more than 24.40 percent, is outside anything the file has ever recorded. That is a materially different sentence from the Harborline one, and the difference is arithmetic rather than confidence.
depth.mistake: The commonest mistake is stress-testing the wrong variable. Advisors routinely test a decline in receipts while leaving the contribution margin fixed at a figure taken from the best month, then report that the file survives. The margin is usually the more fragile assumption, because it is an estimate rather than a document, and a two-point move on a thin-margin file does more damage than a 10 percent revenue swing. The correction is to write the margin with its basis and its date, and to run the margin test explicitly: at Corrigan, a margin of 20 percent instead of 22 percent lowers contribution to $9,692.31 and coverage to 1.20, still above one; at Harborline, a 28 percent margin instead of 30 percent lowers baseline contribution to $7,236.92 and coverage to 1.19, while the September-October trough falls to 0.90. A second mistake is performing the test silently and reporting only the conclusion, which denies the reviewer the chance to check the arithmetic and makes the recommendation look stronger and less credible at the same time.
depth.application: Task: for one live recommendation, write an assumptions table with four rows (receipts, contribution margin, existing debits, schedule start date), each with a figure, a source and a date; then run a one-variable test on each and record the resulting coverage. Compute and state the reversal point in the input's own units. Then pull the last ten to twenty decisions of similar shape and record how many ran below forecast in their first quarter as a proportion. Finally write the two-sentence version for the summary: what would reverse this, and what the evidence base for that number is. Self-review rubric: is every assumption sourced or explicitly labelled an estimate; is the margin tested, not just receipts; is the reversal point a number with units rather than an adjective; is the trough taken from records rather than projected; does the summary say the outcome analysis is a small sample and describe its limits; and does the page avoid any claim that a stress test predicts the future.
depth.summary: Stress-testing is how an advisor earns the right to be believed: put the assumptions on the page with their sources, move one at a time, compute the point at which the answer changes, and check the shape of the past against it. Done properly it sometimes shrinks a recommendation and sometimes confirms it, and both outcomes are useful. The habit transfers beyond funding, because the same structure of sourced assumptions, single-variable sensitivity, an explicit reversal point and a measured base rate is what makes any recommendation arguable on evidence rather than on confidence.

visual.description: A labeled worked sequence showing one recommendation tested by moving one assumption at a time, the value at which coverage reaches one, and the difference between a recommendation that shrinks and one that survives.
steps: Row one - assumptions with sources: weekly receipts from twelve dated statements; contribution margin with its basis and the month it came from; existing weekly debits from payoff letters; the schedule's start week.
Row two - baseline build: monthly receipts x 12 / 52 to weekly; weekly x margin to contribution; combined remittances against contribution to the coverage ratio.

Row three - one-variable moves: receipts down 15 percent, then 25 percent; then the margin down two points with receipts unchanged; record the coverage resulting from each single move and change nothing else.
Row four - the reversal point: solve for the input value at which combined remittances equal contribution, and state it in the input's own units, for example weekly receipts of $20,333.33.
Row five - the calendar: overlay the recorded seasonal trough on the schedule's start week and compute coverage for the opening weeks, not the annual average.

Row six - outcomes analysis: count the similar past decisions that ran below forecast in their first quarter, record it as a proportion with the sample size, and route the result back into the amount and the start date.

lessons.title: Documenting what you told a merchant, and when
lessons.explanation: A conversation that is not recorded is a conversation that will be re-described by whoever needs it to have gone differently. The record you build is not there because someone will sue; it is there because every party, including you, will mis-remember a number that was said out loud six weeks ago. A usable communication record has seven parts: the date and time; who was present and in what capacity; the channel (call, email, in person, text) and whether it was recorded; the substance in figures, meaning the amount in dollars, the total repayment, the per-hundred-dollars cost, the payment and its frequency, the fees, and the schedule's start; what was given in writing and when; what the merchant said and asked back; and what happens next, with a date and the name of who does it. Attach the documents rather than summarising them: the disclosure you sent, the statement months received, the payoff figures, and the UCC search result. Three legal and procedural anchors make the case for this level of care. First, evidentiary signature: a state disclosure regime can require the provider to obtain the recipient's signed acknowledgement, electronic signatures included, on the disclosures at the time the recipient accepts the offer, and Virginia's sales-based financing chapter requires exactly that, together with a disclosure of whether and how much the provider pays a broker, which is precisely the conflict the record should carry. Second, retention with teeth: under Regulation B a creditor retaining records for business credit keeps them for twelve months in general, but for a business whose gross revenues exceeded a million dollars, or for trade credit or credit incident to a factoring arrangement, the floor is at least sixty days after notification, lengthened to twelve months if the applicant requests reasons or retention in writing within that period; and if the notification or statement of reasons was given orally, what must be retained is the notation or memorandum the creditor made. Third, the small-business lending practice standard: SBA expects loan actions to be documented with the request, the justification, the analysis and every document relied upon, memorialised in the loan file, which is a working description of what an advisor's file should contain even where SBA is not involved. None of this makes a broker the creditor, and citing another party's retention rule as if it bound you is itself inaccurate; the rule tells you what good practice looks like and how long the paper will matter. The honest additional point is about the merchant: give them the same record. A dated summary of what was said, in dollars, sent the same day, prevents most disputes and makes the remaining ones short.
lessons.example: On 3 March 2026 you tell a merchant by telephone that a $48,000 advance with a factor of 1.40 carries a total repayment of $67,200, which is $140 per $100 of net proceeds, at $2,584.62 a week over 26 weeks. You email the disclosure the same afternoon listing the disbursement amount after any fees, the finance charge, the total repayment amount, the payment amount and frequency, the schedule start date, all other potential fees, the collateral or security interest position, and the commission you are paid in connection with the offer. The merchant replies at 2:31 p.m. confirming he wants to proceed, and you note the reply. Seven weeks later he disputes two items: $1,150 he says was debited twice, and $6,250 he says he was promised away, because in his account the total repayment was $41,250. Your exposure if the record is blank is $1,150 + $6,250 = $7,400 plus six hours of your time at a $45 opportunity cost, $270, which is $7,670. With the record, the reconstruction is four items, about twenty minutes of work, $15.00, which is 0.20 percent of that exposure. The dates also need to be right, because the retention clock starts on the notification. Notice on 3 March 2026, plus sixty days, is 2 May 2026, the minimum retention for a business over a million dollars in revenue or for factoring-type credit; the merchant's written request for reasons on 20 March 2026 obliges a written statement of reasons within thirty days, which is 19 April 2026, and extends retention to twelve months, 3 March 2027. Two details decide the dispute: the written disclosure restates the total repayment in dollars rather than describing the cost as a rate, and the summary email was sent the same day, so the merchant's account of what he was promised can be checked against a document he received while the conversation was still current. Nothing in the record claims the cost is an interest rate or an annual percentage rate, because a factor is not one, and the note says so in as many words.
lessons.question: A merchant disputes the total repayment seven weeks after funding and says the numbers he was quoted were different. What decides the outcome?
lessons.answer: A same-day written record in dollars, sent to the merchant at the time, with the signed or acknowledged disclosure attached, which converts a memory dispute into a document comparison.
lessons.distractor: The advisor's recollection of the call, since the conversation happened once and the merchant's version arrived later with an amount attached to it.
lessons.correction: Recollection is the weakest available evidence and the easiest to attack, because it belongs to the party with the interest. The document that helps is the one created contemporaneously and given to the merchant: a disclosure in dollars for disbursement, total repayment, per-hundred-dollars cost, payment and frequency, plus any other fees, the schedule start and the collateral position. Regulation B's retention rules and SBA's expectation that loan actions be documented with the request, justification, analysis and documents relied upon both point at the same practice, and neither is a promise about any particular dispute; the point of keeping the record is that the disagreement becomes brief.

depth.definitions: A communication record is a contemporaneous, dated note of what was said and given, with the documents attached. A disclosure is the written statement of terms handed to the merchant before acceptance. Evidencing a disclosure means obtaining an acknowledgement, which some state regimes require in signed or electronic form at the time of acceptance. Retention is how long the paper must be kept; under Regulation B the general figure for business credit is twelve months, with a special business-credit rule of at least sixty days after notification for gross revenues above a million dollars or for trade or factoring-type credit, extended to twelve months on a written request for reasons or retention. A notation is the memorandum a creditor makes when a required statement is given orally, and the notation is what must then be retained. Jurisdiction matters: a state's disclosure and retention requirements apply within that state's scope, and a provider or broker operating elsewhere should not imply that they bind everyone.
depth.mechanism: Documentation works because it changes the type of question that can be asked. Without a record, the dispute is about credibility, an unresolvable contest between two memories, and it will be settled by whoever has more leverage or more patience. With a record, the dispute is about a document's contents, which anyone can read. The second mechanism is temporal: the value of a record decays fast, because details that are obvious on the day of the call are unrecoverable a week later, so the practice has to be same-day or it is not a practice. The third is protective in both directions. A merchant who receives the numbers in dollars is far less likely to have formed a different understanding, so the record prevents as much as it proves. And the advisor who writes the summary is forced to notice what was actually said, which is where a promise like "it's basically twelve percent" either gets caught or gets written down.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting case shows why the substance of the record matters as much as its existence. A second advisor keeps meticulous notes of twenty-two calls, each appropriately dated, and none of them states a single amount. When the same merchant disputes the cost, the notes prove that conversations happened and prove nothing about what was said: the file contains twenty-two pages and no figure. The repair is not more notes but a template with number fields, so that the note cannot be completed without a disbursement amount, a total repayment, a per-hundred-dollars figure, a payment and frequency, the other fees, the schedule start and the collateral position. The second advisor rebuilds the record for the live files at a cost of roughly ninety seconds per note, and discovers a second benefit: on four of eleven open files the note reveals that the merchant was never told the total repayment figure in dollars, only the factor, which is a conversation to have now rather than at funding. That is a 36.36 percent gap rate on a sample of eleven, and it is a number worth recording, because it measures the advisor's own disclosure practice rather than the merchant's understanding.
depth.mistake: The commonest mistake is treating the record as something created for a future dispute rather than as part of the conversation, which produces notes written days later, in summary, without figures. A second is over-correcting into a transcript habit: long reconstructed narratives full of adjectives invite scrutiny of the wrong things and are less reliable than a short dated note with numbers. A third, and the most serious, is letting the record become a substitute for the disclosure itself, so the advisor believes the note protects a transaction in which the merchant was never given the terms in writing at all. The diagnostic is simple: open the file and ask whether a stranger could state, from the documents alone, the disbursement amount, the total repayment, the payment, its frequency, the other fees, the collateral position and the commission. If the answer is no, the record is decoration.
depth.application: Task: build a one-page communication template with the seven parts described, plus number fields for disbursement, total repayment, per-hundred-dollars cost, payment, frequency, other fees, commission and schedule start. Apply it to your next three merchant conversations on the same day, attach the documents, and send each merchant a copy. Then audit the last five files you closed and record how many could be reconstructed from documents alone. Self-review rubric: is every entry dated and attributed; are amounts in dollars with the metric named and never described as a rate or an APR; does the note state what the merchant was told about fees, guarantees, reconciliation and the security interest; does it record what the merchant asked and what you said in reply; does it name the next step and its date; is the commission and its contingency in the record; and is the same copy in the merchant's hands?
depth.summary: A record is the difference between a conversation and an account of a conversation, and only one of them survives scrutiny. Date it, put the numbers in dollars, name the documents you gave, note what the merchant said back, and give them the same version. Retention rules from other people's regimes tell you how long the paper matters and are not themselves your obligation, and a factor is never recorded as a rate. Done this way, documentation stops being defensive paperwork and becomes the plain, dated evidence of a conversation the merchant can re-read.

readings.title: Code of Virginia - Title 6.2, Chapter 22.1 (Sales-Based Financing Providers), sections 6.2-2228 to 6.2-2238
readings.note: Read section 6.2-2231 for the disclosure items: the total amount and the disbursement amount after any fees deducted or withheld at disbursement; the finance charge; the total repayment amount; the estimated number of payments based on projected sales volume; payment amounts and frequency; a description of all other potential fees and charges not included in the finance charge, including draw, late payment, returned payment and prepayment fees; an updated disclosure on early payoff or refinance; a description of collateral requirements or security interests; and item 9, a statement of whether the provider will pay compensation directly to a broker in connection with the offer and the amount of that compensation. Read section 6.2-2232 for the requirement that the provider obtain the recipient's signature, which may be an electronic signature, on all required disclosures at the time the recipient accepts the offer, and section 6.2-2234 for the prohibition on confession of judgment provisions in a sales-based financing contract. Section-specific direction: this is the authority for signed disclosure and broker-compensation disclosure, and it is scoped to recipients whose principal place of business is in Virginia; the lesson says so and does not generalise it. readings.title: CFPB - Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.12 Record retention
readings.note: Read (b)(1) the retention period of twenty-five months, twelve months for business credit, after notification of action taken or of incompleteness, and the retained items: the application and any written or recorded information used in evaluating it, plus a copy of the notification of action taken and the statement of specific reasons if furnished in writing, or, if furnished orally, any notation or memorandum made by the creditor. Read (b)(4) on retention during an investigation or enforcement proceeding until final disposition, and (b)(5) the special business-credit rule: at least sixty days after notifying the applicant of the action taken where gross revenues exceeded a million dollars or for trade credit, credit incident to a factoring agreement or similar business credit, extended to twelve months if the applicant requests reasons or retention in writing within that period. Section-specific direction: the sixty-day floor and the twelve-month extension are the numbers a business-credit file manager needs, and the notation requirement is the reason an oral statement must be written down at the time.
