visual.title: The seven-part communication record and its two clocks
visual.description: A labeled template showing the fields a same-day merchant conversation record needs, the documents that must be attached, and the retention clocks that start when notification is given.
steps: Field block one - identification: date, time, participants and role, channel, and whether the call was recorded.

Field block two - figures in dollars: disbursement amount, total repayment, cost per hundred dollars of net proceeds, payment amount, frequency, all other fees, commission, and the schedule start date. No annualised figure appears in this block.
Field block three - documents: what was sent and when, with the signed or acknowledged disclosure attached, plus statement months, payoff figures and the UCC search result.
Field block four - exchange: what the merchant asked, what was said in reply, and any request refused, with the reason stated.
Field block five - next step: the action, the owner and the date, written in the record on the day.

Clock one - sixty days from notification as the business-credit floor where revenues exceed a million dollars or the credit is factoring-type; a written request for reasons within that window extends retention to twelve months and obliges a written statement of reasons within thirty days.
Clock two - twelve months as the general business-credit retention figure, with the notation or memorandum standing in for any statement given orally.

questions.prompt: You hand your screening framework to a colleague. On the first file, two fields require a document the merchant says he will send next week, and one judgment field is scored at an extreme. What does a working three-state framework output?
questions.answer: Two unresolved fields and one flagged judgment field: the screen returns a not-yet note naming the two documents, placing the extreme judgment score with a named second reader, and stating the amount the evidence in hand actually supports.
questions.distractor: A pass with a note to collect the two documents if the file proceeds, since the merchant has committed to sending them and a not-yet answer will cost the advisor a week of the merchant's patience.
questions.correction: Unresolved is the default wherever the evidence is absent, and it blocks in the same way a fail blocks; treating a promise of a document as evidence moves the check downstream to the funder, where a documentation-driven decline teaches the merchant nothing. The extreme judgment score is a separate output: it does not fail the field, it routes the file to a second reader, which is the mechanism that caught the disagreements in the twenty-file test (agreement rose from 85.00 percent to 95.00 percent at a cost of $225.00, an increase of 16.67 percent over $1,350.00).

questions.prompt: A five-page memo contains fourteen ratios, a page of statement excerpts and a conclusion reading "the file looks sound". The committee sends it back within twenty minutes without a decision. What was missing?
questions.answer: The decision line: an amount, an instrument, a term, a per-hundred-dollars cost, conditions, and the single measured assumption that would reverse the recommendation, with everything that neither supports nor defeats that sentence cut.
questions.distractor: A longer financial information section, because a committee that returns a memo in twenty minutes has not been given enough data to reach a conclusion of its own.
questions.correction: The write-up standard's test is whether the document supports the rating, and its explicit instruction is to present conclusions derived from the financial information rather than recite details from statements. The 90-minute memo at $67.50 exists to replace a round trip; a memo that cannot be decided in one sitting produces the round trip and the delay, which on the Riverton file put the merchant's $1,850 early-payment discount at risk. Data added without a decision line lengthens the meeting rather than shortening it.

questions.prompt: A merchant with a coverage ratio of 2.10 asks for a discount from a factor of 1.36 to 1.30 on a schedule whose repayment period is eleven weeks, to finance a delivery van with a nine-year life. Which diagnosis applies?
questions.answer: A product problem: the repayment period sits far outside the nine-year life of the asset, so the schedule is being paid out of working capital; instrument, amount and schedule shape are the questions, and price is the last one.
questions.distractor: A pricing problem, because a coverage ratio above two means capacity is not in question and the only remaining variable between the offers is cost.
questions.correction: Coverage above one rules out an average-week capacity problem and says nothing about duration. The OCC's structural weakness list names the indicators directly, including repayment plans significantly in excess of the useful life of the asset being financed, and warns that a flaw does not stop being a flaw because it has become the competitive norm. A discount on an eleven-week schedule for a nine-year asset reduces the amount repaid and leaves the mismatch intact; a term facility or a smaller amount is the honest restructuring.

questions.prompt: Your memo recommends $70,000 on a coverage ratio of 1.27 built on the annual average, and the file's own statements show the schedule's opening nine weeks run at 24 percent below that average. What must the memo say?
questions.answer: The trough arithmetic: coverage of 0.97 in the opening weeks with a shortfall of $207.08 a week, the reversal point in dollars of weekly receipts, and a sized-down amount whose coverage holds in the trough rather than on the average.
questions.distractor: The annual figure only, with a note that the merchant has two strong quarters ahead, because the seasonal dip is already reflected in the annual average that produced coverage of 1.27.
questions.correction: A schedule is paid week by week; an average cannot cover a specific week. At Harborline the trough puts contribution at $5,892.92 against $6,100.00 of combined remittances, coverage 0.97, and a $55,000 alternative at the same factor produces $2,750.00 a week, coverage of 1.45 at the baseline and 1.10 in the trough. Stating the reversal point, weekly receipts of $20,333.33, is what makes the recommendation testable rather than merely confident.

questions.prompt: Seven weeks after funding, a merchant disputes a $1,150 duplicate debit and says the total repayment he agreed to was $6,250 lower than the file shows. Which evidence decides it?
questions.answer: The dated record: the same-day note in dollars, the disclosure listing disbursement amount, total repayment, per-hundred-dollars cost, payment and frequency, and the other fees, and the merchant's written acknowledgement of it.
questions.distractor: The advisor's call log, which shows four contacts in the week before funding and establishes that the terms were discussed more than once.
questions.correction: A log proves that conversations occurred and nothing about their content. What resolves the dispute is a document created at the time, given to the merchant, stating the figures in dollars, with the signed or acknowledged disclosure attached; Regulation B's retention provisions, including the special business-credit rule of at least sixty days after notification extended to twelve months on a written request, and SBA's expectation that loan actions be documented with the request, justification, analysis and documents relied upon both point at that practice without binding a non-bank broker as law.

units.title: Holding the line: pressure, over-lending, concentration and the capstone defence

lessons.title: A merchant who pressures you: what to refuse, and how to end a conversation
lessons.explanation: Pressure from a merchant is information, not an instruction. It tells you what the money is for, how much runway is left, and whether the merchant is describing the file or negotiating it. Sort every request into two lists. The first list is servable: speed as far as the actual process allows, a written explanation of a decline, an escalation to a named person at the funder, a call between the merchant and the funder, a smaller amount with a faster decision, a clear statement of what document would move the file, and an honest answer about your own commission. These are requests about process, and process is where you have leverage. The second list is a refusal, and it has a short and stable membership: inflate or round up deposits or revenue; leave an existing advance, lien or judgment out of the application; sign, backdate or alter a document; describe a factor as a rate or an annual percentage rate; promise approval, a timeline, or a specific amount before a funder decides; imply that you have influence over the decision that other applicants do not have; conceal fees until the paperwork; or file a use of proceeds under a description that does not match it. Two authorities make the refusal list concrete without pretending to bind a non-bank broker. SBA's rules on conducting business with it list, as good cause to suspend or revoke an agent's privilege to do business with SBA, giving a guaranty to an applicant that the application will be approved, implying the use of political or other special influence, soliciting services where an undisclosed business relationship exists, and receiving compensation from both the applicant and the lender on the same loan outside a narrow disclosure exception. And the FTC's deception policy states that deception can be an omission of material information, not only a false statement, that the entire transaction or course of dealing is considered rather than one sentence in isolation, that oral representations count, and that a representation is material if it is likely to affect the decision. Nobody has to say anything false for a file to be mis-described: leaving an advance out of the schedule achieves it. Ending a conversation is a skill and it has a shape. Name the constraint in one sentence, without an argument. State what you will do, with a date. Put it in writing the same day. Offer the one alternative that actually exists, even if it is smaller. Decline the part you cannot do, in the same breath as the part you can. Then stop, politely, and do not re-argue: a second and third round of justification reads as room to negotiate, and each round costs both parties time while changing nothing. Ending a call is not a failure of service. Continuing a call you cannot help inside is the failure, because it keeps the merchant's only scarce resource, time, in a conversation that has no outcome.
lessons.example: A merchant with twelve months of receipts averaging $78,000 a month wants $100,000 and asks you to describe deposits as $95,000 a month, saying everyone rounds. The true weekly receipts are 78,000 x 12 / 52 = $18,000.00, and at a 34 percent contribution margin the true weekly contribution is 18,000 x 0.34 = $6,120.00. The inflated figure is 95,000 x 12 / 52 = $21,923.08 a week, roughly 22 percent above the statements. Now run both outcomes rather than arguing about them. If the inflation succeeds and a funder sizes on it, $100,000 at a factor of 1.36 is $136,000 over 26 weeks, $5,230.77 a week, which against the true contribution of $6,120.00 is 85.47 percent, a coverage ratio of 1.17. That looks fundable, which is the point of the request, until receipts fall 15 percent: weekly receipts of $15,300.00, contribution of $5,202.00, coverage of $5,202.00 / $5,230.77 = 0.99, a shortfall of $28.77 a week, $748.00 across the 26-week schedule. The merchant asked for the version of the deal that breaks. If the file is submitted on the statements, the same structure is sized to roughly $70,000 over 26 weeks at the same factor, which is $3,661.54 a week, 59.83 percent of true contribution, coverage 1.67, and it survives the same 15 percent decline at coverage 1.42. The refusal is not a matter of taste; it is arithmetic the merchant can check. On the call itself, ending it well costs less than continuing it badly: four rounds of pressure at 22 minutes each is 88 minutes, $66.00 at a $45 opportunity cost, plus a 20-minute written summary at $15.00, $81.00; three further rounds would add roughly $49.50 and change nothing. The advisor's commission on $100,000 at three percent would be $3,000, which is why the pressure is worth resisting out loud: the commission is paid on the funded amount, the shortfall of $748.00 is paid by the merchant, and the honest note says both numbers.
lessons.question: A merchant asks you to describe $78,000 of monthly deposits as $95,000, adding that the funder's own software rounds figures anyway. What is the correct response?
lessons.answer: Refuse in one sentence, explain that a filing built on a rounded figure is a misrepresentation of the file and would fail on verification, offer the amount the statements support, and send a same-day written note recording the request and the refusal.
lessons.distractor: Describe the deposits as the merchant's stated figure with a note that it is unverified, since the funder will request its own statements and can make its own determination.
lessons.correction: An unverified figure presented as the applicant's revenue is the misrepresentation, and a note does not cure it: deception can consist of an omission or a course of dealing, and the entire transaction is considered, not one disclaimer line. The arithmetic is also against it. On the inflated number a $100,000 advance at a factor of 1.36 consumes 85.47 percent of the true weekly contribution; the same file at honest statements supports about $70,000 at 59.83 percent and survives a 15 percent fall in receipts at coverage 1.42, where the inflated version lands at 0.99 with a $28.77 weekly shortfall. Refuse, then offer the version that holds, and record both in writing the same day.

depth.definitions: Pressure in this lesson means a request that either asks for a change in the facts as presented or tries to keep a conversation alive after it has no available outcome. A servable request is about process: timing, information, escalation, a written explanation, a smaller amount, a call with the funder, or a straight answer about the advisor's compensation. A refusal is a request that requires misrepresenting the file, promising an outcome someone else decides, or implying influence that does not exist. Materiality means the information is likely to affect the recipient's decision. An omission is the failure to disclose information whose absence makes the rest misleading. A course of dealing is the whole pattern of conduct and representations, which is what an enforcement analysis considers. A guarantee of approval is an assurance of an outcome the giver cannot control, and SBA treats giving one as good cause to revoke an agent's privilege to conduct business with SBA.
depth.mechanism: The reason to sort requests rather than simply push back is that each category has a different correct answer, and the refusal becomes credible only when it arrives alongside a served request. A merchant hears a flat no as a dead end; a merchant hears "not that, and here is what I can do with a date" as a route, and the pressure drops because the underlying need is time or an amount, not the specific misstatement. The second mechanism is incentive symmetry. The advisor is paid on a funded transaction and the merchant carries the servicing consequence, so the advisor's own resistance to the request is weaker than the merchant's need, which is exactly why the refusal must be put in writing and in dollars. The third mechanism is conversational. Pressure tactics depend on the other party continuing to engage: each justification offered is treated as evidence that the position can move. Ending the exchange after one clear statement removes the thing being optimised for, and it does so without discourtesy, which matters because the same merchant may return with a fundable file and because a reputation for caving under repetition travels.
depth.secondExample: The contrasting case is a merchant whose pressure is entirely legitimate, and misreading it as a tactic is the error. A trucking company with $146,000 a month in receipts, fourteen months of history and clean obligations is facing a supplier deadline: a deposit of $38,000 is due in nine days for two replacement tractor units, and a failure to pay it loses a $4,600 contract discount already negotiated. Weekly receipts are 146,000 x 12 / 52 = $33,692.31, contribution at 27 percent is $9,096.92, and existing debits of $2,880 a week. A $38,000 advance at a factor of 1.34 over 20 weeks is $50,920 / 20 = $2,546.00 a week, which is $134 per $100 of net, combined $5,426.00, 59.65 percent of contribution, coverage 1.68. Nothing here is a request to change the file. The deadline is a document, not a mood: the supplier's written deposit notice with a date. The correct response is to serve it: state the date in the submission, name the verification that will be run, and say plainly that the timeline is not guaranteed, since only a funder decides. If the nine days cannot be met, the honest answer names the alternative that can be, which here is a smaller bridging amount or a renegotiated deposit with the supplier, and the file stays clean in both versions.
depth.mistake: The commonest mistake is answering a refusal request by arguing about consequences, which invites a debate the advisor can lose and lengthens the call. The fix is to state the rule once, in the first person, without narrative. A second mistake is the soft version of complicity: agreeing to "round" a figure, or leaving an obligation out because it will be paid off before funding, or describing a factor as "close to" a rate, each of which is small enough to feel harmless and is exactly the kind of thing that later looks deliberate. A third is failing to record the request itself: a note that records only the refusal cannot show what was asked, and the pattern of requests is the fact that matters if the relationship ends badly. A fourth, specific to the cash advance context, is letting urgency license a bad product; urgency is a reason to act quickly on the honest structure, never a reason to skip verification.
depth.application: Task: write your own two lists, servable and refused, in your own words, with the sentence you will actually use for each refused item; then take a recorded or remembered pressure conversation and rewrite it as a three-move close: the constraint in one sentence, what you will do with a date, the alternative that exists, and the written summary sent the same day. Self-review rubric: is each refusal stated as what you will not do rather than as an accusation about the merchant; does every refusal come with the servable item that addresses the underlying need; is anything promised about approval, timing or amount, which nothing may be; is the merchant's own cost side stated in dollars where the request has arithmetic consequences; is the request itself recorded, not only your answer; and does the note avoid any instruction or implication that facts may be softened if the file looks strong?
depth.summary: Pressure is a signal to be classified, not a mood to be endured. Serve what is about process, refuse what is about the facts or someone else's decision, state the refusal once in the first person, offer the real alternative, and close the conversation in writing the same day. The arithmetic is what makes the refusal credible and the commission line is what keeps it honest, because the advisor profits from the funded amount while the merchant carries the schedule.

readings.title: FTC Policy Statement on Deception (14 October 1983, appended to Cliffdale Associates, 103 F.T.C. 110, 174 (1984)), Sections I and II
readings.note: Read the Summary section for the three elements: a representation, omission or practice that is likely to mislead; the perspective of a consumer acting reasonably in the circumstances; and materiality, meaning the practice is likely to affect the decision. Read Section II for the statements that most matter to a financing conversation: most deception involves written or oral misrepresentations or omissions of material information, deception may occur in other conduct associated with a sales transaction, the entire advertisement, transaction or course of dealing is considered, the issue is whether the practice is likely to mislead rather than whether it actually deceived anyone, and some cases involve an omission whose disclosure is necessary to prevent the claim or sale from being misleading. Section-specific direction: use this to justify refusing to present an unverified figure as revenue and to justify recording what was actually said, since oral representations count. The statement is a policy statement about consumer-facing practices; the lesson applies its logic to a commercial financing conversation and does not claim it is a rule binding a broker in a business-to-business transaction. readings.note: Read paragraphs (b), (d), (e) and (g). Paragraph (b) makes soliciting services to an applicant where an undisclosed business relationship exists good cause for suspension or revocation; paragraph (d) covers implying or stating that the work will include political or other special influence, with the examples including use of the words Small Business Administration in a way that implies endorsement and "giving a 'guaranty' to an Applicant that the application will be approved"; paragraph (e) makes a fee that does not bear a necessary and reasonable relationship to services rendered good cause, while noting that a fee based solely on a percentage of a loan or guarantee amount can be reasonable depending on the circumstances; paragraph (g) states the two-master prohibition with its limited disclosure exception. visual.title: Two lists and a three-move close
visual.description: A labeled decision aid that routes a pressured request either to a process answer with a date or to a stated refusal, then closes the exchange in writing the same day.
steps: Route step one - what is the request about: timing, information, escalation, a smaller amount, or an explanation (servable); or a change in the facts, a promise about someone else's decision, or implied influence (refused).
Servable column - assign an owner and a date, and put the answer in writing: what will be submitted, what will be verified, and what cannot be promised.
Refused column - one sentence in the first person, no argument, naming what you will not do and why in plain terms, for example that figures presented as revenue must come from statements.

Cost line - where the request has arithmetic consequences, show them in dollars: for example coverage of 1.17 that falls to 0.99, a shortfall of $28.77 a week, against coverage of 1.67 that survives the same decline.
Disclosure line - state the commission and its contingency in the same conversation, so the merchant can weigh the advice against the advisor's interest.
Close - stop after one statement and one alternative, do not re-argue, and send the dated summary recording the request, the refusal, the alternative and the next step.

lessons.title: Multi-product merchants and the risk of over-lending
lessons.explanation: A merchant with one facility is the exception. The typical file arrives with a bank term loan, an equipment lease, a line of credit attached to a deposit account, a merchant advance already running, a supplier's trade terms, and a personal card the owner uses for business. Each of these was approved by someone who looked at the business, and none of them was approved by anyone who looked at the sum. Over-lending is what happens when a series of individually reasonable decisions is never added together, and the diagnosis is not moral but arithmetic: aggregate the weekly obligations, measure them against contribution, and test the total in the worst recorded month. Three supervisory ideas transfer. First, leverage relative to norms: the FDIC's examination manual defines a transaction as leveraged when the obligor's post-financing leverage, measured by debt-to-assets, debt-to-equity or cash flow to total debt, significantly exceeds industry norms for leverage, and it expects a bank to apply its own bank-wide, consistent definition so that aggregate exposure can be identified and monitored. An advisor who places files can apply the same discipline in plain English: how much total debt does this business carry per dollar of monthly receipts, and how does that compare with the other merchants of its kind in my own book? Second, de-levering capacity: the same manual expects underwriting to consider the loan's purpose and sources of repayment and the capacity to de-lever over a reasonable period, and to analyse a leveraged borrower's past and current performance against projections, including the assumptions behind those projections. Third, the marginal question: what does the next facility actually cost the merchant in weekly dollars, and what does it buy? A new advance that funds a payroll bridge over eight weeks but is repaid over twenty-six is not a bridge; it is a second obligation with a bridge's name. Two operational consequences follow. The first is arithmetic honesty at the aggregate level: a merchant at 55 percent of contribution before a new facility has very little room, because a fixed remittance does not fall when receipts do. The second is documentary: aggregate every obligation in the memo with its remaining balance, its weekly or monthly payment, its payoff figure and any filed lien, and state the total. If a merchant will not disclose one, the file has an unresolved field, and the honest answer is a not-yet rather than a smaller number that pretends the obligation is absent.
lessons.example: Delgado Landscaping asks for $45,000 to bridge eight weeks of payroll while a municipal contract is invoiced. The file already shows a bank term loan at $2,300 a week, two equipment leases totalling $1,850 a week, and one running advance at $2,750 a week, which is $6,900 a week of existing obligations. Monthly receipts average $164,000, so weekly receipts are 164,000 x 12 / 52 = $37,846.15, and contribution at 33 percent is 37,846.15 x 0.33 = $12,489.23. Existing obligations are 6,900 / 12,489.23 = 55.25 percent of contribution before anything new. The requested facility at a factor of 1.34 over 22 weeks is 45,000 x 1.34 / 22 = $2,740.91 a week, which is $134 per $100 of net proceeds. Combined, 2,740.91 + 6,900 = $9,640.91, or 77.19 percent of contribution, coverage 12,489.23 / 9,640.91 = 1.30. Now test the season rather than the average. Winter receipts in this file run 25 percent below the annual figure: weekly receipts of $28,384.62, contribution of $9,366.92, against the same $9,640.91 of obligations, coverage 0.97 and a shortfall of $273.99 every week of the trough. Without the new facility the same trough gives coverage of 9,366.92 / 6,900 = 1.36. That single comparison is the whole argument: the new advance does not merely add cost, it moves the merchant from surviving the worst quarter with room to missing it every week, and the failure mode is a missed remittance in the same month the contract is invoiced but not yet paid. The purpose test says the same thing from the other direction: the payroll need is 45,000 / 8 = $5,625.00 a week of use, and the facility remits $2,740.91 a week, so over the eight weeks it returns 2,740.91 x 8 = $21,927.27, which covers 48.73 percent of the need in the same period while adding a 22-week obligation to the schedule. The honest answer is a smaller amount sized to the trough, a schedule that starts after the invoice is expected to be paid, or a bank facility whose draw matches the payroll timing. Each of those is a real option; "it is only $45,000" is not.
lessons.question: A merchant already carries $6,900 a week of obligations against $12,489.23 of weekly contribution and asks for a new advance that would take the total to $9,640.91 a week. Coverage on the annual average is 1.30. What does the file actually support?
lessons.answer: Less than requested: at the recorded 25 percent winter trough contribution falls to $9,366.92, coverage 0.97 and a $273.99 weekly shortfall, so the amount must be sized to the trough or the schedule must start after the invoice is paid.
lessons.distractor: The amount requested, because a coverage ratio of 1.30 on the annual figure is within the house floor and the merchant's municipal contract is a documented source of repayment.
lessons.correction: A fixed remittance does not flex with receipts, so the annual average is the wrong denominator for a decision that is paid weekly. At the trough the same obligations leave coverage at 0.97 with a $273.99 shortfall, and without the new facility the trough coverage is 1.36, which is the comparison that shows what the advance costs the merchant in resilience rather than only in dollars. The documented contract is a source of repayment for the business, not a shock absorber for a schedule, and the honest recommendation names the sized amount, the start date and the trough arithmetic.

depth.definitions: Over-lending is a condition in which the aggregate obligations of a business exceed what its cash flow can service across the range of its normal year, even though each facility was individually supportable when approved. Aggregate obligations are every scheduled payment the business owes, whatever the instrument, including leases and trade terms with fixed instalments. Contribution is receipts less direct costs. De-levering capacity is the ability to reduce total debt out of operating cash flow over a stated period, and it is the reason a leveraged structure is judged against the plan to reduce it. Marginal cost is the change in weekly obligations attributable to the new facility alone. Undisclosed obligation is an existing payment or lien the merchant declines to document; within this course it is an unresolved field, not a smaller number.
depth.mechanism: Over-lending is a structural consequence of how credit is sold and recorded: each facility is originated by a different party, measured against the business at a different moment, and stored in a different system, so nobody is positioned to see the sum. The business experiences that sum as a weekly drain that does not react to its own volatility, which produces a specific and predictable failure pattern: the merchant is current through the strong season and misses payments in the weak one, then takes a further facility to cover the miss, which raises the drain again. The mechanism is therefore self-reinforcing, and the intervention point is before the second facility. Two measurements capture it. The first is the trough ratio: aggregate obligations against contribution in the worst recorded period, because both are known from the file rather than projected. The second is purpose-to-payment timing: whether the money is used at roughly the pace it is repaid, since a mismatch of a factor of two means the business funds the facility out of operating cash flow for the whole term.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting file shows a genuinely additive second facility, and the arithmetic is what distinguishes it. Rosales Produce runs $310,000 a month in receipts, contribution at 19 percent because it is a distributor, and existing obligations of $7,400 a week; it asks for $60,000 to buy a refrigerated unit that will move 30 percent of a rental contract in-house. Weekly receipts are 310,000 x 12 / 52 = $71,538.46 and contribution is $13,592.31, so existing obligations are already 54.44 percent of contribution. The new facility at a factor of 1.31 over 30 weeks is 60,000 x 1.31 / 30 = $2,620.00 a week, combined $10,020.00, which is 73.71 percent of contribution and coverage 1.36; at the recorded 15 percent summer trough, contribution falls to $11,553.46 and coverage to 1.15, still above one. That is not the whole case, because the money changes the business: hiring out the refrigerated transport costs $2,910.00 a week in the current contract, so the new facility replaces a larger recurring cost with a smaller fixed one and raises contribution by about $290.00 a week before any volume effect, which improves the trough ratio instead of degrading it. The same measurement, the trough ratio, supports the second facility here and refuses it in the Delgado file, which is the point: the arithmetic is indifferent to how many products a merchant already has and decisive about what the next one does to the worst week of the year.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is measuring the new facility against the business as though the existing obligations were not there, which happens because the existing payments are described as temporary, about to be refinanced, or paid by a family member. The correction is to include everything scheduled, with its payoff figure, and to treat any obligation the merchant will not document as unresolved. A second error is treating a higher factor on a second position as the main risk, when the real risk is the shape of the aggregate: adding fifteen basis points of cost to a schedule that already consumes 55 percent of contribution is a smaller problem than adding a further $2,740.91 a week of fixed drain. A third error is assuming that a bigger business can absorb more, which ignores that contribution margin often falls as revenue grows in distribution and contracting, so a larger file can sit closer to the line than a small one.
depth.application: Task: build an aggregate obligations table for one live file: every instrument, its remaining balance, its payment and frequency, its payoff figure, any filed lien, and its weekly equivalent. Sum it, divide by weekly contribution for the baseline and for the file's recorded trough, and then compute the marginal effect of the proposed new facility in the same two states. Add a purpose-to-payment line: what the money is used for per week against what the schedule repays per week. Self-review rubric: is every obligation sourced to a document with a date; is any undisclosed obligation carried as unresolved rather than omitted; is the trough taken from records; is the marginal cost stated in dollars and per hundred dollars of net proceeds with no annualised figure; is the purpose-to-payment ratio stated honestly even where it is unfavourable; and does the recommendation name the amount, the start date and the condition that would change the answer?
depth.summary: Over-lending is an arithmetic fact about a collection of reasonable decisions that were never added up, and the tool that finds it is the aggregate obligations table measured against contribution in the worst recorded period rather than the average. The purpose test tells you whether the next facility is doing what it claims; the trough test tells you what it costs the merchant in resilience. Both are indifferent to how many products the merchant already holds, which is why they work where product-by-product underwriting does not.

lessons.title: Portfolio thinking: noticing your own concentration as an advisor
lessons.explanation: An advisor who places files is running a portfolio whether or not anyone calls it that, and the portfolio has the same failure mode as a lender's: a single shared sensitivity that makes many files perform badly at the same time. Concentration is not a synonym for size. A pool of exposures shares a characteristic or a sensitivity, and when that characteristic is triggered, the transactions react together. Regulatory practice offers three transferable ideas, with the caveat that the thresholds are written for banks and bind nobody else. First, a concentration is defined in OCC terms as the sum of direct, indirect or contingent obligations exceeding 25 percent of tier 1 capital plus the allowance for loan and lease losses, and the same booklet insists that size alone is not the risk: the difference in a pool's performance metrics between normal and stressful times is a direct measure of risk, and a smaller pool with a wide range of outcomes can be riskier than a larger, more diversified one. Second, limits and sublimits: where a limit is set for a broadly defined pool, prudent practice includes sublimits for material groups inside it, so that a broadly defined category does not hide a sharply defined exposure. Third, a limit on size alone is a weak instrument; the booklet describes banks combining a size limit with a credit-risk benchmark, for example defining a pool as material when its exposure exceeds a stated percentage of capital and its adversely rated share exceeds a stated percentage of the pool. Translated into an advisor's own book, the pools that matter are the ones an advisor can name: industry or business type, geography, product type, a single funder, a single processor, a single referral source, one ISO relationship, and the merchants who share a seasonal calendar. The measurement is mechanical. Count and total the placements by pool, express each pool as a share of volume and of commission, record which pools share a sensitivity with each other, and set a limit that is a decision rather than a number you have already exceeded. Then ask the stress question in the smallest useful form: if this pool's merchants all renewed, defaulted or stopped trading in the same quarter, what share of my income stops with them? That question is answerable with a spreadsheet, and its answer usually changes the next three placements rather than the next thirty. Two honesty requirements attach. The bank thresholds are cited as borrowed reasoning, not as obligations, and an advisor who quotes a tier 1 capital ratio at a merchant is using language that does not apply. And concentration is not only about risk: it is also about competence. An advisor who places only restaurant deals knows that industry's seasons, which is a real edge, and the argument for limits is not that the edge is imaginary but that it is correlated.
lessons.example: Yvette placed 34 files last year: 11 restaurants and cafes, 7 trucking and freight, 6 retail, 5 salons, and 5 in everything else. Gross volume was $3,296,666.67 across the five pools, and her commission at three percent of gross was $98,900.00. Restaurants contributed $1,118,000 of gross, which is 1,118,000 / 3,296,666.67 = 33.91 percent of volume and $33,540.00, also 33.91 percent of the $98,900.00 commission. Trucking was $742,000, 22.51 percent; retail $661,000, 20.05 percent; salons $388,000, 11.77 percent; other $387,666.67, 11.76 percent. Her average restaurant deal was 1,118,000 / 11 = $101,636.36. Now apply the two questions the framework exists to answer. First, is the pool above her own limit? She writes a rule of no more than 25 percent of placed volume in any one pool, which would have capped restaurants at 3,296,666.67 x 0.25 = $824,166.67 and left $293,833.33 to be placed elsewhere. Second, what happens if the pool reacts together? Her eleven restaurants are concentrated in one metropolitan area and mostly serve lunch trade near the same employment district, so they share one sensitivity: employment in that district. If a single large employer moves out and restaurant placements fall to four deals in the following year at the same average size, gross restaurant volume is 4 x 101,636.36 = $406,545.45 and commission falls to $12,196.36, a loss of $21,343.64 against the prior year, which is 21.58 percent of her total commission. Nothing about her skill changed; her income fell by more than a fifth because one sensitivity moved. The same exercise on trucking flags a second kind of concentration that a count would miss: the seven freight files were placed with three funders, but five of them sit with the same funder, so a change in that funder's appetite would affect five files at once and 15.15 percent of her placements, and the same funder holds both of her two largest files. Her revised framework keeps the 25 percent pool limit, adds a sublimit of 15 percent of placements with any single funder, and records a shared-sensitivity note for the restaurant and salon pools, which both depend on the same district's foot traffic.
lessons.question: An advisor's placements are 33.91 percent restaurants in one employment district, and five of seven freight files sit with one funder. What has this framework found?
lessons.answer: Two concentrations sharing different sensitivities: a pool above the advisor's own 25 percent volume limit with a single geographic employer dependence, and a funder concentration where a change in one appetite affects 15.15 percent of placements at once.
lessons.distractor: Healthy specialisation: a deep presence in one industry and a strong relationship with one funder are the two advantages an advisor builds deliberately over years.
lessons.correction: Specialisation and concentration are the same fact read for two different purposes, and both readings are true. The edge is real, which is why the limit is about the share rather than the pool's existence. What the measurement adds is the paired exposure: the restaurant and salon pools share the district's foot traffic, so a single employment event touches both, and the freight files share one funder's appetite, so a credit-policy change reaches five placements at once. A limit turns a preference into a decision made in advance instead of a position discovered afterwards.

depth.definitions: A concentration in this lesson is a pool of placements that shares a characteristic or a sensitivity to the same economic, financial or business development, so that their performance tends to move together, whether or not that characteristic is a formal risk factor. Volume concentration is a pool's share of amounts placed; income concentration is its share of the advisor's commission, and the two can differ when deal sizes differ. A sublimit is a limit inside a broader limit. Shared sensitivity is a characteristic two different pools have in common, such as one geography or one employer. An advisor's own book is the set of placements made, maintained and renewed by that advisor, as distinct from a lender's portfolio. The OCC's 25 percent-of-capital threshold and the interagency CRE criteria are bank supervisory measures; the lesson cites them as borrowed reasoning with no application to a non-bank advisor's obligations.
depth.mechanism: Concentration risk accumulates quietly because each placement is defensible on its own and no single one looks like a pattern. The mechanism that makes it dangerous is correlation: pools that look different on paper reveal the same underlying dependence when the event arrives, so the loss or the drop in volume is not spread across many independent bets but concentrated in what turns out to be one. In an advisor's book the outcome is income volatility rather than credit loss, and the same structure produces it, because renewal revenue and referrals depend on the same merchants continuing to trade. There is a second mechanism specific to advisory work: the pools an advisor knows best keep growing because they are the ones being handled well, which is precisely how a book becomes correlated without anyone choosing correlation. Setting a limit in advance is the intervention that survives this, because the limit is a decision made when the advisor is calm rather than a judgement made when a promising file is on the phone.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting book shows the same measurement producing sublimits rather than a stop. Cole has 41 placements totalling $2,180,000: 9 agricultural files at 21.95 percent of volume, 8 construction at 19.50 percent, 7 medical and dental practices at 17.06 percent, 6 restaurants at 14.66 percent, and 11 others at 26.83 percent combined. No pool breaches 25 percent, so a naive reading of the framework says the book is diversified. The sublimit test inside the construction pool says otherwise: six of the eight construction files are in residential remodelling, which is 14.63 percent of volume but 75.00 percent of the construction pool, and all six depend on the same housing turnover; and inside the agricultural pool, five files are in one crop. The granular reading is what changes behaviour: Cole sets a sublimit of 12 percent of volume for any single subsegment, which the residential remodelling files already exceed at 14.63 percent, and starts routing new remodelling enquiries to a second market while taking on no specialisation outside agriculture. That is 8-10 percentage points of patience rather than a refusal, and it is exactly the pattern the OCC booklet describes when it says limits for broadly defined pools should include sublimits for material groups of segmented exposures inside them.
depth.mistake: The commonest mistake is measuring concentration by count rather than by amount and sensitivity, which hides the pool that matters: twenty small salon files can be a smaller exposure than five large freight files, and two industries that look distinct can share one employer, one landlord or one seasonal calendar. The second mistake is treating the funder relationship as exempt from concentration because it feels like loyalty or pipeline; a single funder's policy change is one decision that can affect many placements at the same time. The third is quoting bank thresholds as if they applied: a tier 1 capital ratio and a 100 percent or 300 percent risk-based capital criterion are supervisory measures for banks, and using them to describe an advisor's own book misleads the merchant and the reviewer alike. The diagnostic that catches all three is to write the sensitivity next to the number: for each pool, one sentence stating what single event would make many of its merchants behave the same way.
depth.application: Task: build a one-page concentration worksheet for your own placements over the last twelve months. List every placement with amount, commission, industry, geography, product, funder, processor and referral source. Total by pool and express each as a share of volume and of commission. On a second page, write the shared-sensitivity sentence for each pool and mark any two pools that share an event. Set one size limit per pool and one sublimit for the largest subsegment inside the largest pool, dated, and describe in three lines what you will do differently when the next enquiry would breach either. Self-review rubric: are shares computed on both volume and commission; is every pool's sensitivity named in plain words; is the funder dimension included; are the limits set below what the book already shows rather than above it; are borrowed supervisory thresholds labelled as borrowed; and does the page say plainly that a limit is a decision about patience and not a claim about any merchant's credit quality?
depth.summary: Portfolio thinking converts an advisor's book from a list of wins into a set of correlated exposures, and the transferable technique is simple: pool the placements, measure shares of volume and income, name the sensitivity each pool shares, and set limits and sublimits before the next enquiry arrives. The regulatory thresholds for banks supply the reasoning and not the obligation. The point is not that specialisation is wrong, but that the same knowledge that makes an advisor effective in one pool is what makes the book react as one when that pool's environment moves.

lessons.title: When to walk away, and how to say so in a way that is useful
lessons.explanation: Declining is a normal output of the work, and most advisors are worse at it than at recommending. The first task is to know which kind of no you are giving, because they are not interchangeable. A permanent disqualifier is not a no today; it is a no under any structure, and the honest version says so and gives a reason. A capacity no says the amount does not fit the cash flow, and it comes with a number that does fit. A documentation no says the evidence is not in the file yet, and it comes with a list and a date. A conduct no is the file where the merchant wants the facts arranged, which is a refusal to work rather than a decline of the file, and it should be stated in the same calm register as the others. A conflict no is the one advisors rarely name: where the advisor's own compensation is the reason the recommendation would be a bad one, the honest answer is to disclose the conflict and either hand the file over or step out, and it is worth naming aloud because a reviewer will find it anyway. Two legal structures shape how a decline is delivered. Under Regulation B a completed business-credit application for a business with gross revenues above a million dollars gets the action taken communicated within a reasonable time, orally or in writing, with a written statement of reasons if the applicant requests it in writing within sixty days; below a million dollars, and for business credit generally, the notification content and the statement-of-reasons mechanics follow the standard provisions, including the rule that reasons must be specific and that internal standards or a failure to reach a qualifying score are not a sufficient statement of reasons. And the credit standard itself is not the advisor's invention: for SBA-guaranteed lending the applicant must be creditworthy, the loan must be so sound as to reasonably assure repayment, and the analysis must be the prudent, generally acceptable commercial credit analysis used on similar non-guaranteed loans; a decline written against that standard is a professional act, not a courtesy. The write-up that accompanies a decline should therefore do four things: state the decision; give the specific reason in the file's own terms, with figures; name what would change the answer and by when; and say what happens next to the documents. Close the loop with the merchant in writing, keep the record, and leave the relationship in a condition where a different, smaller or later request can be considered on its merits. The sentence to avoid is any version of "you will never get funded", which is a prediction about other people's decisions, and the sentence to keep is a description of this file, this evidence, this amount and this date.
lessons.example: Selby's Mill asks for $48,000 and refuses to supply three of the twelve statement months, saying the missing months were weak and that a smaller sample tells the same story. The advisor's walk-away is not a mood, it is a decision with a number attached. If the file is submitted anyway, the costs on the merchant's side are ten statement reprints at $5.00 each, $50.00, a non-refundable third-party processing fee of $1,750.00, and seven hours of the owner's time at a $45.00 opportunity cost, $315.00, which is $2,115.00 of exposure on a file whose central figure cannot be verified. The advisor's commission if it somehow funded would be 48,000 x 0.03 = $1,440.00, which is 68.09 percent of the merchant's exposure, and the advisor's downside on the same file is zero. That asymmetry is the reason the walk-away is written down rather than performed silently: a file where the advisor risks nothing and stands to earn $1,440.00 while the merchant risks $2,115.00 is a file the advisor should not be the one to submit. The written decline goes out on the day of the decision, dated 6 March 2026, with a specific reason in the file's terms: the deposits cannot be verified across the requested amount because three of twelve statement months were not supplied, so repayment capacity cannot be assessed against the standard of prudent commercial credit analysis rather than against any house preference. It names what would change the answer, with dates: statement months four to nine, delivered by 15 April 2026; the satisfaction letter for the outstanding judgment, whenever it is granted; and a UCC search the advisor will order at no cost to the merchant. It states the process facts honestly: because the business's gross revenues exceed a million dollars, the decision is communicated within a reasonable time and the written statement of specific reasons is provided on written request within sixty days, which the merchant makes on 20 March 2026, putting the statement of reasons due by 19 April 2026; and the retention clock on the notification runs to 5 May 2026 at minimum, extended to 6 March 2027 by that written request. The last line offers what exists: a re-application in the week of 20 April 2026 on the fuller evidence, at an amount the statements support, which the advisor will size when the months arrive.
lessons.question: A merchant with $1.4 million of revenue refuses to supply three of the twelve requested statement months and asks you to submit what you have. What is the defensible action?
lessons.answer: Decline to submit, send a dated written decision naming the unverifiable repayment capacity as the specific reason, list the documents and dates that would change it, and offer a re-application date with the amount the fuller evidence would support.
lessons.distractor: Submit with the nine months available and disclose the gap in the submission, since the funder can decide what weight the missing months deserve and the merchant has asked to proceed.
lessons.correction: Disclosing a gap does not cure it: the advisor would be submitting a file whose central figure cannot be assessed, at a cost of $2,115.00 to the merchant in statement fees, a non-refundable processing fee and time, against a $1,440.00 commission to the advisor with no downside if it fails. The standard the decline is written against is that the applicant be creditworthy and the analysis be the prudent commercial credit analysis used on similar loans, and repayment capacity is exactly what the missing months would evidence. The useful version of the no carries the four elements: decision, specific reason, what would change it and when, and what happens next.

depth.definitions: A decline, a refusal and a not-yet are three different outputs. A decline rejects the file as presented; a not-yet defers it pending named evidence or a later date; a refusal to work rejects the conduct of the transaction, such as a request to omit an obligation. A permanent disqualifier bars a programme regardless of structure. A capacity no is accompanied by an amount that does fit. A statement of specific reasons is the written explanation of adverse action whose content, under Regulation B, must be specific and may not consist of internal standards or policies or a reference to failing a qualifying score. The sixty-day window is the period within which a business-credit applicant whose revenues exceed a million dollars may request reasons in writing. Retention runs from notification and, for business credit in that revenue band or for factoring-type credit, lasts at least sixty days, extended to twelve months by a written request for reasons or retention.
depth.mechanism: A decline performed well produces information and preserves options; a decline performed badly produces a rumour and closes the door. The mechanism that makes the written version better is that it separates the outcome from the assessment: the merchant can disagree with the outcome but still use the reasons, because reasons are actionable in a way that a mood is not. The second mechanism is the loop between the advisor's incentive and the file's prospects. Because compensation is contingent on funding and the merchant's costs are not, every file carries a pressure to submit, and writing the decline with the merchant's own exposure figure in it converts that pressure into a visible number. The third is retention and process: a dated decision, delivered within a reasonable time, with the reasons and the retention clock understood, is the difference between a disputed file and a file that can be re-opened on new evidence.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting walk-away shows the third kind, the conflict no, where the file might fund and the advisor still steps out. A merchant files a $220,000 request through the advisor's own referral relationship with a funder that pays a higher commission than the alternatives and whose structure, on this file, produces a schedule of 220,000 x 1.37 / 30 = $10,046.67 a week against weekly contribution of $14,900.00, which is 67.43 percent of contribution, coverage 1.48, in a business whose recorded trough is 22 percent below average. The trough contribution is 14,900 x 0.78 = $11,622.00, and the trough coverage is $11,622.00 / $10,046.67 = 1.16, so the file is not hopeless: a smaller amount or a share-of-receipts structure would sit comfortably. The conflict is that the advisor's commission is 1.4 times higher on this funder's structure than on the alternative that fits the trough better. The honest action is to disclose the difference in dollars, present both structures, recommend the one with the higher trough coverage, and offer to pass the file to a colleague if the merchant would rather not rely on the recommendation. That is stepping out of the conflict rather than out of the deal, and it is the version of walking away that a reviewer cannot attack, because the file shows the arithmetic and the compensation side by side.
depth.mistake: The commonest mistake is declining in a way that predicts the future, for example telling a merchant that no funder will take this file or that he should come back in a year, both of which are claims about other people's decisions made by someone who cannot make them. The second is the soft decline, where the advisor says the file is with underwriting and lets the merchant wait on a decision that was never submitted, which costs the merchant the one resource the decline was supposed to protect. The third is failing to record the reason and the date, so that a complaint later has to be answered from memory. The fourth is treating a capacity no as a permanent one and losing a merchant who would be fundable at a smaller amount six weeks later with a fuller file; the diagnostic for all four is the same four-element test: decision, specific reason with figures, what changes it and when, and what happens next.
depth.application: Task: write a decline template with the four elements and use it on a real or archived file. Include the decision and its date, the specific reasons drawn from the file's own figures, the documents or events that would change the answer with dates, the process facts the merchant is entitled to know in your jurisdiction, the next step for the documents, and the amount and timing of any alternative that exists. Add a conflict line stating what you are paid and on what contingency. Self-review rubric: does the reason name evidence or capacity rather than internal standards or a score; is there no prediction about any other decision-maker; is the amount that would fit stated as a figure rather than as an invitation to try again; is the merchant's own cost exposure on a failed attempt given in dollars; is the date of the decision recorded alongside the notice; and does the letter avoid any suggestion that the merchant should change how the file is described?
depth.summary: Walking away is a competent output, and the useful version is written, dated and specific. Say which kind of no it is, give the reason in the file's own figures, name what would change it and when, keep the record the process requires, and leave an alternative on the table where one exists. The two failure modes to avoid are predictions about other people's decisions and soft holds that keep a merchant waiting on a file nobody submitted, and both are avoided by the same four-element structure.

visual.title: Four kinds of no and the four-element decline
visual.description: A labeled decision aid that classifies why a file is being declined and produces a written decline containing the decision, the specific reason, what would change it, and what happens next.
steps: Sort step - is this a permanent disqualifier, a capacity problem, a documentation problem, a conduct problem, or the advisor's own conflict? The five categories have different remedies and different letters.
Element one - the decision and its date: declined, not yet, or refused, stated plainly, with a record that the notice went out within a reasonable time.

Element two - the specific reason in the file's own figures: for example deposits unverifiable across the requested amount because three of twelve statement months are missing, never internal standards and never a score threshold.
Element three - what would change the answer: named documents or events with dates, plus the amount the fuller evidence would support.
Element four - what happens next: the re-application window, who orders the search, what the merchant should send and by when, and what is paid for by whom.
Conflict line - what the advisor is paid and on what contingency, stated in dollars, so the merchant can weigh the recommendation against the interest behind it.
Ledger line - the merchant's exposure on a failed attempt in dollars, against the advisor's commission, so the asymmetry is recorded rather than assumed.

lessons.title: Capstone: defending a recommendation, then answering a hostile reviewer's strongest objection
lessons.explanation: A recommendation is finished when it has been defended twice: once against your own assumptions, and once against someone whose job is to find the weakest link and pull. The defence has six parts, in this order, and every one of them is a sentence rather than a section. What is being decided, in one line with amount, instrument, term and cost per hundred dollars of net proceeds. Which two or three facts carry it, each with a source and a date. The arithmetic, shown so it can be recomputed, including the trough and not only the average. The conditions, each of which could fail. The reversal assumption, in the units of the input, with the value that changes the decision. And your own interest, in dollars, with what it depends on. A hostile reviewer works from a different starting point than a friendly one: not "is this reasonable" but "where does this break". Supervisory practice calls that effective challenge and describes it as critical analysis by objective, informed parties who can identify limitations and produce appropriate changes, depending on a combination of incentives, competence and influence. When the reviewer is inside your own firm the incentives are usually present; when the reviewer is at a funder or a regulator the reviewer's interest is different from yours, and the strongest objections tend to have a recognisable shape. Three shapes cover most of them. The first is the alternative history: your trough is the worst period you have seen, and the reviewer has seen a worse one. The second is the unverified input: your contribution margin is an estimate, and the reviewer will not treat an estimate as a fact. The third is the omitted obligation: something scheduled that the file does not contain, whether because the merchant did not disclose it or because a document was never requested. A prepared advisor answers each in one of three ways, and the choice is the skill. Concede and change the decision, when the objection reduces the amount or alters the structure; that is the outcome the process exists to produce. Concede the point and keep the decision, when the objection is real but does not move the number below the floor, and say so using the reviewer's own figure. Or dispute the fact with a document, which requires that the document exist in the file at the moment of the meeting rather than being promised afterwards. What must never happen is defending the recommendation because it is yours. The reviewer is testing the file; treat the objection as data about the file and the argument disappears. Disagreement should also be recorded rather than resolved by seniority: supervisory practice expects a written explanation when a reviewer disagrees with the recommended classification, and the informal rule that accompanies it, write it up when in doubt, is the reason this capstone ends with a note rather than a conversation. Finally, the defence should state what the recommendation is not. It is not an approval, not a prediction, and not a claim about any other decision-maker's answer.
lessons.example: Ostrander Auto Body asks for $120,000 for a second spray booth and produces sixteen months of statements. Monthly receipts average $186,000, so weekly receipts are 186,000 x 12 / 52 = $42,923.08, and the contribution margin is estimated at 29 percent from two years of financials plus the owner's cost schedule, which gives weekly contribution of $12,447.69. Existing obligations are $5,900 a week, which is 47.40 percent of contribution. The recommendation is $75,000 at a factor of 1.33 over 24 weeks: 75,000 x 1.33 = $99,750, or 99,750 / 24 = $4,156.25 a week, which is $133 per $100 of net proceeds, and with the existing obligations the combined figure is $10,056.25, which is 80.79 percent of contribution with coverage of 1.24. The file's own autumn dip is 19 percent below the annual average: weekly receipts of $34,767.69, contribution of $10,082.63, and coverage of exactly 1.00, which is the reason the recommendation carries a condition rather than a clean yes. Now the hostile reviewer speaks. "Your worst case is nineteen percent because that is the only history you have. In the year you did not see, the dip was thirty-one percent, and this is a discretionary repair business, so the dip is the risk." The arithmetic answers it without argument. At 31 percent, weekly receipts are $29,616.92 and contribution is $8,588.91, so the combined remittances of $10,056.25 produce coverage of $8,588.91 / $10,056.25 = 0.85 and a shortfall of $1,467.34 a week. At the house floor of 1.20 on the reviewer's stressed case, allowed combined remittances are 8,588.91 / 1.20 = $7,157.42, which leaves room of 7,157.42 - 5,900 = $1,257.42 a week, supporting 1,257.42 x 24 / 1.33 = $22,690.34 of net proceeds. The objection is conceded and the decision changes: $22,700 at the same factor, or the same recommendation restructured as a share-of-receipts facility that falls with receipts, or a deferred start until the spring. The memo records the objection in the reviewer's own words, the two computations side by side, and the revised recommendation, together with what would restore the larger amount: a second year of monthly statements covering a full autumn, or a signed contract with the dealership that supplies the booth's work. The lesson is not that the reviewer was right about the future; it is that the reviewer found the assumption the advisor had the least evidence for, and the file is now sized against a stress nobody has observed. The same defence would have been run the other way if the numbers had held: at Cole's distributor file a 20 percent fall left coverage at 1.06 and the reversal point was a 24.40 percent decline, twice the file's worst year, which is a concession that keeps the decision and says so in the reviewer's own units.
lessons.question: Your recommendation is $75,000 with coverage of 1.24 on the annual average, 1.00 at the observed 19 percent seasonal dip. A reviewer says the real dip is 31 percent. What is the correct response?
lessons.answer: Concede the objection, show that at 31 percent coverage falls to 0.85 with a $1,467.34 weekly shortfall, and revise the recommendation to the amount the reviewer's stressed case supports, $22,700 at the same factor, or to a share-of-receipts structure, recording both in the memo.
lessons.distractor: Defend the file by explaining that the observed dip is the only measured history and that the reviewer is substituting a projection for evidence, then restate the original recommendation.
lessons.correction: The objection is precisely about the limits of the evidence, which is the strongest available attack and the one the reviewer is entitled to make: the file has one autumn, and the contribution margin is an estimate. Answering it with the record's authority misses the point. The arithmetic settles it: at 31 percent, contribution is $8,588.91 against $10,056.25 of remittances, coverage 0.85, and a floor of 1.20 supports $22,690.34 of net proceeds at the same factor. Conceding and changing the decision is the successful outcome here; a defence that refuses to move leaves the merchant with a schedule that fails in the reviewer's scenario and the advisor with an unrepaired objection.

depth.definitions: A recommendation is a conditional decision that includes the evidence, the conditions and the reversal assumption. A hostile reviewer is a reviewer whose incentive is to find the weakest link; effective challenge is the supervisory term for critical analysis by objective, informed parties able to identify limitations and produce change. An alternative-history objection substitutes an unobserved stress for the observed record. An unverified-input objection attacks an estimate treated as a fact. Conceding the point while keeping the decision means agreeing the stress is real and showing it does not breach the floor. The reversal assumption is the input value at which the decision changes. Documentation of disagreement is the written record that a reviewer reached a different conclusion, which supervisory practice expects where management disagrees with a classification; the accompanying informal rule is to write it up when in doubt.
depth.mechanism: A defence works when it is structurally identical to an audit: the same facts, the same arithmetic, the same stated assumption, so that a reviewer can recompute rather than assess. That is why the ordering matters more than the wording, and why the reversal assumption belongs in the summary rather than in a footnote: it tells the reviewer where to push, which paradoxically defuses most attacks, because an advisor who has already named the weakest point is harder to surprise and easier to believe. The three available responses to an objection are also the mechanism for keeping the process honest. Conceding and changing the recommendation is available only if the reviewer's number is testable, so the advisor's first move is to compute it rather than argue about it; conceding and keeping is available only if the floor is stated in advance, so the floor must be written down before the meeting; and disputing a fact requires a document in the file, which is a reason to gather evidence rather than promise it. Recording the disagreement preserves the file's value after the meeting, because the next reviewer will read the note, and it protects both parties from a later dispute about who said what.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting defence test shows the second objection shape, the unverified input, and it is answered with a document rather than with an argument. Kwon Fabrication asks for $95,000 and the memo's arithmetic rests on a 34 percent contribution margin, which came from a single good quarter. The reviewer objects that the margin is an estimate and that at 28 percent the schedule is much tighter. Rather than defend the quarter, the advisor pulls the last eight quarters and computes the range: contribution margins of 36, 35, 34, 34, 33, 31, 30 and 29 percent, a minimum of 29 percent. At 29 percent, weekly contribution on receipts of $39,000 is $11,310, existing obligations are $3,400, and the proposed remittance of 95,000 x 1.32 / 30 = $4,180 gives combined $7,580 and coverage of 1.49, comfortably above the floor of 1.20. The objection is conceded and the decision stands, and the memo is stronger for it because the 29 percent figure is the advisor's own worst recorded quarter rather than a preference. Had the margin floor been 24 percent, the same computation would have produced coverage of 1.24 and the answer would have been to reduce the amount, which is the same test applied with a different result. What makes the second version persuasive is that the concession is real: the memo states that the original 34 percent was not representative, names the eight-quarter range, and uses the minimum for the decision.
depth.mistake: The commonest mistake is defending the number rather than the file, which turns a review into a status contest and ends with a decision made by seniority rather than by arithmetic. The second is the silent concession: adjusting the amount after the meeting without recording why, so the file shows two inconsistent recommendations and no reason for the change. The third is answering an alternative-history objection with the authority of the record, when the whole objection is that the record is short; the correct move is to compute the reviewer's scenario and see what it supports. The fourth is failing to state the floor in advance, which makes conceding-and-keeping unavailable and forces every objection into a win or lose choice. The diagnostic that catches all four is the four-line test: is the decision stated with an amount; is the strongest objection written down in the reviewer's words; is the reviewer's scenario computed rather than resisted; and does the note say what would restore the original amount?
depth.application: Task: take your strongest live recommendation and prepare a one-page defence: the six parts in order, the two or three carrying facts with sources, the arithmetic including the trough, the conditions, the reversal assumption in the input's units, and your own compensation. Then write the three objections you would raise if you were paid to find the file's weakest point, in the reviewer's voice, and compute each one. Decide for each whether you concede and change, concede and keep, or dispute with a named document that is already in the file. Record the result as a dated addendum. Self-review rubric: is the decision a single line with amount, term and cost per hundred dollars of net proceeds; is every figure traceable to a document with a date; is the trough computed and not quoted from memory; is the reversal assumption a number with units; is the strongest objection written down in the reviewer's own words; is the response to each objection computed rather than asserted; is any disagreement recorded rather than settled informally; and does the page state that the recommendation is conditional and that nothing in it constitutes an approval, a rate or a prediction?
depth.summary: A recommendation is not finished until it has survived the strongest objection someone else can build against it, and the technique is to compute that objection instead of arguing with it. Six parts in a fixed order, an objection written in the reviewer's words, one of three responses chosen deliberately, and the result recorded as a dated addendum turn a defence from a contest of confidence into a computation either party can check. The transferable part is the habit: the reviewer's role is to find the assumption with the least evidence, and an advisor who finds it first, names it in the summary and states the value at which the answer changes is doing the same work in advance.
